TOOL {"type": "reasoning", "id": "rs_08e791b925547dcf016a9461f870c087d2807240503125223c", "summary": ["**Re-outputting new notes verbatim**"], "content": []}
ASSISTANT You are right about the mismatch, with one correction:

\[
\eta_n\sqrt n\to0
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
\eta_n=o(n^{-1/2}),
\]

not \(\eta_n=o(\sqrt n)\).

The earlier headline was sharp for the simplified toy system, whose GD-to-flow error is only \(O(\eta_n)\). But it was not stated in the stronger learning-rate regime certified by the full neural-network proof. Below is the corrected, full-proof-compatible version of the toy argument.

# Headline result

Let

\[
(p_i,z_{i,0}),\qquad i=1,\ldots,n,
\]

be independent copies of \((P,Z_0)\), where \(P\in\{-1,1\}\). The label \(p_i\) remains fixed; only \(z_{i,k}\) is trained.

Define

\[
\phi(z)=\arctan z,
\qquad
f_{n,k}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\phi(z_{i,k}),
\qquad
r_{n,k}=f_{n,k}-y.
\]

Exact finite-width GD is

\[
z_{i,k+1}
=
z_{i,k}
-
\eta_n p_i r_{n,k}\phi'(z_{i,k}).
\]

Use the physical clock

\[
t=k\eta_n.
\]

Assume

\[
\eta_n+\eta_n\sqrt n+\eta_n^2n\longrightarrow0.
\]

Equivalently, it is enough to assume

\[
\eta_n\sqrt n\longrightarrow0.
\]

The limiting population state is

\[
\mu_t=\operatorname{Law}(P,X(t)),
\]

where

\[
F(z)=z+\frac{z^3}{3},
\qquad
X(0)=F(Z_0),
\qquad
Z(t)=F^{-1}(X(t)).
\]

Its residual and dynamics are

\[
r(t)=\mathbb E[P\phi(Z(t))]-y,
\]

\[
\frac{dX(t)}{dt}=-P\,r(t).
\]

This is autonomous: the current law \(\mu_t\) determines \(r(t)\), and \(r(t)\) determines the next movement.

For every fixed \(T\) and every fixed bounded function \(\psi(p,z)\) that is Lipschitz in \(z\),

\[
\boxed{
\sup_{0\le t\le T}
\left|
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\psi(p_i,z_i^{\mathrm{GD}}(t))
-
\mathbb E[\psi(P,Z(t))]
\right|
\longrightarrow0
\quad\text{in probability}.
}
\]

Choosing

\[
\psi(p,z)=p\phi(z)
\]

gives convergence of the prediction, residual, and normalized loss.

---

## 1. Raw finite GD versus transformed finite flow

Let

\[
q(z)=\phi'(z)=\frac1{1+z^2},
\qquad
X=F(z)=z+\frac{z^3}{3}.
\]

Because

\[
F'(z)=\frac1{q(z)},
\]

the raw continuous gradient flow

\[
\dot z_i=-p_i r_nq(z_i)
\]

becomes exactly

\[
\dot X_i=-p_i r_n.
\]

The coordinate transformation is exact in continuous time, but not for discrete GD.

Let

\[
v_i=-p_i r_n.
\]

One GD step is

\[
z_i^+=z_i+\eta_nq(z_i)v_i.
\]

Since \(F\) is cubic,

\[
\begin{aligned}
F(z_i^+)
={}&F(z_i)+\eta_n v_i
\\
&+\eta_n^2z_iq(z_i)^2v_i^2
+\frac{\eta_n^3}{3}q(z_i)^3v_i^3.
\end{aligned}
\]

In the toy system, \(|v_i|\) is uniformly bounded, so the accumulated GD-to-flow error is \(O(\eta_n)\).

The full neural-network proof has a backpropagated field whose normalized norm is bounded, but whose largest coordinate may be \(\sqrt n\) times larger. Its one-step coordinate defect is therefore bounded by

\[
C_T\left(\eta_n^2\sqrt n+\eta_n^3n\right).
\]

There is also an ordinary ODE local defect \(O_T(\eta_n^2)\). Over approximately \(T/\eta_n\) steps, stability gives

\[
\sup_{t\le T}
d_n\!\left(
\theta_n^{\mathrm{GD}}(t),
\theta_n^{\mathrm{flow}}(t)
\right)
\le
C_T\left(
\eta_n+\eta_n\sqrt n+\eta_n^2n
\right).
\]

Thus the first approximation vanishes under

\[
\eta_n\sqrt n\to0.
\]

For the toy model this condition is stronger than necessary, but it makes the consolidated statement compatible with the full proof.

---

## 2. Finite flow versus coarse finite Euler

Choose an auxiliary proof mesh \(\delta>0\), independent of \(\eta_n\).

Finite transformed Euler is

\[
X^n_{i,m+1}
=
X^n_{i,m}-\delta p_i r^n_m,
\]

where

\[
r^n_m
=
\frac1n\sum_j
p_j\phi\!\left(F^{-1}(X^n_{j,m})\right)-y.
\]

The transformed vector field is bounded and Lipschitz. Ordinary Euler analysis therefore gives

\[
\sup_{t\le T}
\max_i
|X_i^{n,\mathrm{flow}}(t)-X_i^{n,\mathrm{Euler}}(t)|
\le
C_T\delta,
\]

uniformly in \(n\).

Thus

\[
\text{raw GD}
\approx
\text{finite Euler}
\]

with error at most

\[
C_T\left(
\eta_n+\eta_n\sqrt n+\eta_n^2n+\delta
\right).
\]

The coarse scheme has only

\[
M=\left\lceil\frac T\delta\right\rceil
\]

updates, which is fixed while \(n\to\infty\).

---

## 3. Pop Euler and the finite oracle

Pop Euler is

\[
r_m
=
\mathbb E\!\left[
P\phi(F^{-1}(X_m))
\right]-y,
\]

\[
X_{m+1}=X_m-\delta P r_m.
\]

The finite oracle starts from the same finite initialization as finite Euler but uses the pop residual:

\[
\bar X_{i,m+1}
=
\bar X_{i,m}-\delta p_i r_m.
\]

Its empirical residual is

\[
\bar r^n_m
=
\frac1n\sum_i
p_i\phi(F^{-1}(\bar X_{i,m}))-y,
\]

but the oracle does not use this number in its updates.

Let

\[
E_m=\max_i|X^n_{i,m}-\bar X_{i,m}|.
\]

Subtracting the finite-Euler and oracle updates gives

\[
E_{m+1}
\le
E_m+\delta|r^n_m-r_m|.
\]

Insert \(\bar r^n_m\):

\[
|r^n_m-r_m|
\le
|r^n_m-\bar r^n_m|
+
|\bar r^n_m-r_m|.
\]

Because \(\phi\circ F^{-1}\) is 1-Lipschitz,

\[
|r^n_m-\bar r^n_m|\le E_m.
\]

Therefore

\[
E_{m+1}
\le
(1+\delta)E_m
+
\delta|\bar r^n_m-r_m|.
\]

Since \(E_0=0\),

\[
\max_{m\le M}E_m
\le
(e^T-1)
\max_{m\le M}|\bar r^n_m-r_m|.
\]

Thus finite Euler is close to the oracle whenever the oracle’s residual sampling error is small.

---

## 4. Oracle sampling versus pop Euler

The pop residual sequence

\[
r_0,\ldots,r_{M-1}
\]

is deterministic once the initial population law is fixed.

Each complete oracle trajectory is therefore a deterministic function of its own initialization:

\[
(p_i,\bar X_{i,0})
\longmapsto
(p_i,\bar X_{i,0},\ldots,\bar X_{i,M}).
\]

Hence the complete oracle trajectories are independent copies of the pop Euler trajectory.

At every step \(m\),

\[
p_i\phi(F^{-1}(\bar X_{i,m}))
\]

are independent copies of

\[
P\phi(F^{-1}(X_m)).
\]

Hoeffding’s inequality and a union bound give, with probability at least \(1-\alpha/2\),

\[
\max_{m\le M}|\bar r^n_m-r_m|
\le
\pi
\sqrt{
\frac{\log(4(M+1)/\alpha)}{2n}
}.
\]

Consequently,

\[
\max_{m\le M}E_m
\le
(e^T-1)\pi
\sqrt{
\frac{\log(4(M+1)/\alpha)}{2n}
}.
\]

There is also a separate sampling error for the chosen observable \(\psi\). Let

\[
B_\psi=\sup\psi-\inf\psi.
\]

With probability at least \(1-\alpha/2\),

\[
\max_{m\le M}
\left|
\frac1n\sum_i\psi(p_i,\bar Z_{i,m})
-
\mathbb E[\psi(P,Z_m)]
\right|
\le
B_\psi
\sqrt{
\frac{\log(4(M+1)/\alpha)}{2n}
},
\]

where

\[
\bar Z_{i,m}=F^{-1}(\bar X_{i,m}),
\qquad
Z_m=F^{-1}(X_m).
\]

The first sampling term controls residual feedback. The second controls the empirical \(\psi\)-avg directly.

For complete trajectories, define

\[
\Gamma_i
=
(p_i,\bar Z_{i,0},\ldots,\bar Z_{i,M}),
\]

and

\[
\Gamma=(P,Z_0,\ldots,Z_M).
\]

The \(\Gamma_i\) are independent copies of \(\Gamma\). Therefore, for every integrable trajectory observable \(\Psi\),

\[
\frac1n\sum_i\Psi(\Gamma_i)
\longrightarrow
\mathbb E[\Psi(\Gamma)].
\]

Independence is across complete particle trajectories, not across time within one trajectory.

---

## 5. Pop Euler versus pop flow

The pop flow is

\[
\dot X(t)=-P r(t),
\qquad
r(t)=\mathbb E[P\phi(F^{-1}(X(t)))]-y.
\]

Write

\[
X(t)=X_0-Ps(t).
\]

Then

\[
\frac{ds(t)}{dt}
=
\mathbb E\!\left[
P\phi(F^{-1}(X_0-Ps(t)))
\right]-y.
\]

The right-hand side is bounded and 1-Lipschitz in \(s\), so this scalar ODE has a unique global solution. Therefore the pop flow is well-defined and autonomous.

Pop Euler is ordinary Euler for this same equation. Its error satisfies

\[
\max_{m\delta\le T}|s_m-s(m\delta)|
\le
\frac R2(e^T-1)\delta,
\qquad
R=\frac\pi2+|y|.
\]

Because

\[
X_m=X_0-Ps_m,
\qquad
X(t)=X_0-Ps(t),
\]

the same estimate controls \(X_m-X(m\delta)\). Including the movement between grid points gives

\[
\sup_{t\le T}
|X^{\mathrm{pop\ Euler}}(t)-X^{\mathrm{pop\ flow}}(t)|
\le
C_T\delta.
\]

---

## 6. Add the five errors

For any time \(t\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
&
\left|
\frac1n\sum_i\psi(p_i,z_i^{\mathrm{GD}}(t))
-
\mathbb E[\psi(P,Z(t))]
\right|
\\
&\le
|\text{finite GD avg}-\text{finite flow avg}|
&&\text{(actual step)}
\\
&\quad+
|\text{finite flow avg}-\text{finite Euler avg}|
&&\text{(finite mesh)}
\\
&\quad+
|\text{finite Euler avg}-\text{oracle avg}|
&&\text{(feedback)}
\\
&\quad+
|\text{oracle avg}-\text{pop Euler avg}|
&&\text{(sampling of }\psi\text{)}
\\
&\quad+
|\text{pop Euler avg}-\text{pop flow avg}|
&&\text{(pop mesh)}.
\end{aligned}
\]

If \(\psi\) is \(L_\psi\)-Lipschitz in \(z\), the five terms are bounded by

\[
L_\psi C_T
\left(
\eta_n+\eta_n\sqrt n+\eta_n^2n
\right),
\]

\[
L_\psi C_T\delta,
\]

\[
L_\psi(e^T-1)\pi
\sqrt{
\frac{\log(4(M+1)/\alpha)}{2n}
},
\]

\[
B_\psi
\sqrt{
\frac{\log(4(M+1)/\alpha)}{2n}
},
\]

and

\[
L_\psi C_T\delta.
\]

Therefore, with probability at least \(1-\alpha\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
&
\sup_{t\le T}
\left|
\frac1n\sum_i\psi(p_i,z_i^{\mathrm{GD}}(t))
-
\mathbb E[\psi(P,Z(t))]
\right|
\\
&\le
L_\psi C_T
\left(
\eta_n+\eta_n\sqrt n+\eta_n^2n
\right)
\\
&\quad+
2L_\psi C_T\delta
\\
&\quad+
\left[
L_\psi(e^T-1)\pi+B_\psi
\right]
\sqrt{
\frac{\log(4(M+1)/\alpha)}{2n}
}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Now:

1. Choose \(\delta\) small enough to control both mesh errors.
2. Keep \(\delta\) fixed and take \(n\to\infty\).
3. The learning-rate term vanishes because

   \[
   \eta_n\sqrt n\to0.
   \]

4. The two sampling terms vanish because \(M\) is fixed.
5. Finally let \(\delta\to0\).

This proves uniform compact-time convergence in probability.

The theorem in the audited document fixes

\[
\eta_n=n^{-2},
\]

which satisfies

\[
\eta_n\sqrt n=n^{-3/2}\to0.
\]

More generally, the displayed proof estimate closes for every learning-rate sequence satisfying

\[
\eta_n=o(n^{-1/2}).
\]

Coordinate calculations reveal no further randomness.\n\nWhen the two input Gram matrices are invertible, Gaussian orthogonal projection gives\n\n\\[\nW\\mid\\mathcal H\\ \\overset d=\nY(V^\\top V)^{-1}V^\\top\n+U(U^\\top U)^{-1}Q^\\top P_{V^\\perp}\n+P_{U^\\perp}\\widetilde W P_{V^\\perp}.\n\\tag{1}\n\\]\n\nFor a new input h, put alpha_n=(V^T V)^(-1)V^T h and h_perp=h-V alpha_n. The transpose formula is identical with the two sides interchanged.\n\nAssume for the moment that all limiting input Gram matrices are positive definite. Induction on the finite transcript proves joint W_2 empirical convergence: all coefficients in (2) converge by the previous induction hypothesis; the removed projection has conditional mean squared normalized norm rank(U)/n; after removing it, conditional averaging of independent Gaussian coordinates gives joint weak convergence and second-moment convergence. Globally Lipschitz coordinate instructions preserve W_2 convergence. This works unchanged with two interleaved matrices.\n\n## Why the response coefficient is the source derivative\n\nHere is the identification step, rather than an invocation of a general tensor-program theorem. Use lowercase letters for the limiting scalar variables. Let the previous forward inputs be v_r, and the previous transpose inputs be u_s. Let Gamma_U=(E u_s u_t)_{st}. By induction write\n\n\\[\ny_r=\\xi_r+\\sum_s D_{rs}u_s,\n\\qquad D_{rs}=\\mathbb E\\partial_{\\zeta_s}v_r,\n\\]\n\\[\nq_s=\\zeta_s+\\text{a linear combination of previous forward inputs}.\n\\]\n\nUnavailable/future-source derivatives are zero. Let alpha be the limiting least-squares coefficients and h_perp=h-sum_r alpha_r v_r. Orthogonality gives E[v_r h_perp]=0 for every old forward input. Therefore the non-Gaussian correction in every q_s drops out of its pairing with h_perp:\n\n\\[\n\\mathbb E[q_s h_\\perp]=\\mathbb E[\\zeta_s h_\\perp].\n\\]\n\nThe Gaussian group zeta is independent of the roots and all other Gaussian groups and has covariance Gamma_U. Gaussian integration by parts yields\n\n\\[\n\\mathbb E[\\zeta h_\\perp]\n=\\Gamma_U\\,\\mathbb E\\nabla_\\zeta h_\\perp.\n\\]\n\nThus (2)'s limiting coefficient is\n\n\\[\n\\beta=\\mathbb E\\nabla_\\zeta h\n       -\\sum_r\\alpha_r\\mathbb E\\nabla_\\zeta v_r.\n\\]\n\nAfter substituting the decompositions of y_r into (2), their old responses cancel the second term. The resulting rule is exactly\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\quad\n(Wh)_{\\mathrm{lim}}\n=\\xi_h+\\sum_s u_s\\,\\mathbb E\\partial_{\\zeta_s}h.\n\\quad}\n\\tag{3}\n\\]\n\nThe new Gaussian source is xi_h=sum_r alpha_r xi_r+sigma g_scalar, where sigma^2=E h_perp^2. Hence Cov(xi_h,xi_r)=E[h v_r] and Var(xi_h)=E h^2. The fresh scalar innovation is independent of every old source. As a result, source groups belonging to distinct oriented matrices W, W^T remain mutually independent, even though W and W^T themselves are dependent. The same argument applies separately to A_0 and B_0 at every interleaved call.\n\nThis proof uses the complete derivative of h as its finite coordinate expression. It does not discard derivative paths passing through calls to the other matrix.\n\n## Removing singular-Gram difficulties\n\nFor each matrix call, temporarily replace its input h by h+epsilon chi, where chi is a new independent standard Gaussian input vector, revealed immediately before that call. At fixed epsilon>0, the limiting squared distance of a new input from its previous same-direction input span is at least epsilon^2: project the new independent chi off that fixed-dimensional span and use conditional second-moment calculations. Consequently all limiting query Gram matrices are positive definite, and the preceding proof applies. The chi variables are additional independent roots; the source rule (3) applies to the perturbed query inputs.\n\nFor the fixed finite program, couple perturbed and unperturbed calculations using the same original matrices and roots. The event has probability tending to one. The matrix bound follows, for example, by a fixed-net Gaussian tail bound and a union bound over the two matrices.\n\nThe scalar source constructions converge as epsilon decreases to zero as well. A detailed finite induction suffices: source covariance entries are second moments of previously constructed inputs; Gaussian covariance square roots are continuous even at singular positive-semidefinite matrices; all previously constructed scalar coordinate functions and their source derivatives are continuous in the finite deterministic coefficient list. Their first derivatives have deterministic bounds at each fixed instruction because the coordinate instructions have bounded first derivatives. Therefore Gaussian coupling, W_2 convergence, and dominated convergence pass both second moments and expected source derivatives to the epsilon=0 recursion. No inverse or pseudoinverse is used in this last continuity step. Combining this fact with (4) identifies the unperturbed empirical limit with (3).\n\nFor completeness, degenerate Gaussian Stein also directly explains the absence of ambiguity. If zeta has covariance Gamma and u has second-moment matrix Gamma, then\n\n\\[\n\\mathbb E[\\zeta f]=\\Gamma\\mathbb E\\nabla f,\n\\qquad\nu^\\top(I-\\Gamma^+\\Gamma)v=0\\quad\\text{a.s.}\n\\]\n\nfor every deterministic v. Thus replacing E grad f by Gamma^+ E[zeta f] may change its entries, but cannot change the response sum u^T E grad f. One must not assert convergence of finite pseudoinverses at a rank drop.\n\n## Application and the empirical training coefficients\n\nUnroll A_k and B_k into their initial matrices plus their finite learned rank-one sums. Consequently\n\\[\n B_2=d(Z^{(2)}_0)\n       \\bigl(c_3\\phi(Z^{(2)}_0)+\\sigma_3G^{\\mathrm b}_2\\bigr),\n\\]\n\\[\n \\sigma_2^2:=\\mathbb E[B_2^2]\n =\\mathbb E\\left[d(Z^{(2)}_0)^2\n          \\bigl(c_3^2\\phi(Z^{(2)}_0)^2+\\sigma_3^2\\bigr)\\right]>0.\n                                                                    \\tag{12}\n\\]\n\nFor the second application, condition on the bottom initialization,\n\\(Z^{(2)}_0=W^{(2)}_0H^{(1)}_0\\), and the entire independent initial\nmatrix \\(W^{(3)}_0\\). The field \\(B_2\\) is then fixed and introduces\nno further information about the conditional residual of\n\\(W^{(2)}_0\\). Formula (10) therefore gives\n\\[\n P_1=c_2H^{(1)}_0+\\sigma_2G^{\\mathrm b}_1,\\qquad\n c_2=\\frac{\\mathbb E[Z^{(2)}_0B_2]}{m_1}\n =\\frac{c_3}{m_1}\n       \\mathbb E[Z^{(2)}_0d(Z^{(2)}_0)\\phi(Z^{(2)}_0)]>0. \\tag{13}\n\\]\nHere \\(G^{\\mathrm b}_1\\) is standard Gaussian, independent of\n\\(Z^{(1)}_0\\); the successive fresh innovations can be chosen as\nindependent groups in the canonical initial source construction.\nThe factor \\(c_3\\) in (13) retains the return through the third-layer\nmatrix. Treating \\(B_2\\) as an independent centered multiplier would\nlose this term.\n\nOnly initial finite Gaussian queries are involved in (10)--(13).\nTheir contractions converge by conditional Gaussian averaging: the\nforward activation averages are bounded; in the transpose step the\nrank-one projection error vanishes in normalized \\(L^2\\); bounded\ngates preserve that convergence. Pairwise contractions then converge\nby Cauchy--Schwarz. This calculation uses no trained-state limit.\n\nBy (12)--(13), \\(P_1\\ne0\\), \\(B_2\\ne0\\), and \\(\\beta_3\\ne0\\)\nin their \\(L^2\\) spaces. Moreover,\n\\[\n \\mathcal A^{(2)}_0\\succeq m_1I,\\qquad\n \\mathcal A^{(3)}_0\\succeq m_2I.                         \\tag{14}\n\\]\nFor any nonzero \\(v\\), the first inequality implies\n\\(\\|\\mathcal A^{(2)}_0v\\|\\ge m_1\\|v\\|\\), by taking its inner\nproduct with \\(v\\); the second gives the corresponding bound with\n\\(m_2\\). Finally, multiplication by \\(d(Z^{(\\ell)}_0)\\) has zero\nkernel because \\(d(z)>0\\) for every finite \\(z\\). These observations\nprove the strict positivity asserted after (7).\n\n## Physical time, kernel blocks, and squared speeds\n\nLet \\(f(s)=\\langle W^{(4)}(s),H^{(3)}(s)\\rangle_3\\).\nEquation (6) gives \\(f(s)=m_3s+o(s)\\). In a sufficiently small\nneighborhood of zero, \\(f(s)<1\\), so define physical time by\n\\[\n \\frac{ds}{dt}=2(1-f(s)),\\qquad s(0)=0.\n\\]\nEquivalently,\n\\(t(s)=\\int_0^s[2(1-f(u))]^{-1}\\,du\\). It follows that\n\\[\n s(t)=2t+o(t),\\qquad 1-f(s(t))=1+o(1).                  \\tag{15}\n\\]\nThis is precisely the residual factor for squared loss \\((f-1)^2\\).\nIn particular, with the left-hand sides evaluated at feature time\n\\(s(t)\\),\n\\[\n Z^{(\\ell)}-Z^{(\\ell)}_0=2t^2V_\\ell+o(t^2),\\qquad\n H^{(\\ell)}-H^{(\\ell)}_0=2t^2D_{\\ell,0}V_\\ell+o(t^2).\n\\]\n\nDefine the four population kernel blocks at physical time \\(t\\) by\n\\[\n \\kappa_1(t)=\\|D_1q^{(1)}\\|_1^2,\\quad\n \\kappa_2(t)=\\|H^{(1)}\\|_1^2\\|\\delta^{(2)}\\|_2^2,\\quad\n \\kappa_3(t)=\\|H^{(2)}\\|_2^2\\|\\delta^{(3)}\\|_3^2,\\quad\n \\kappa_4(t)=\\|H^{(3)}\\|_3^2,\n\\]\nwhere every right-hand side is evaluated at \\(s=s(t)\\). Put\n\\[\n \\gamma_1=\\|D_{1,0}P_1\\|_1^2>0,\\qquad\n \\gamma_2=m_1\\|B_2\\|_2^2>0,\\qquad\n \\gamma_3=m_2\\|\\beta_3\\|_3^2>0.\n\\]\nThen\n\\[\n \\kappa_\\ell(t)=4\\gamma_\\ell t^2+o(t^2)\\quad(\\ell=1,2,3),\n \\qquad \\kappa_4(t)=m_3+o(1).                           \\tag{16}\n\\]\nIn particular all three hidden kernel blocks are strictly positive\nat every sufficiently small positive time. These coefficients are\nfinite using only the second moments established above. For example,\n\\[\n \\gamma_1=\\mathbb E\\left[d(Z^{(1)}_0)^2\n           \\bigl(c_2^2\\phi(Z^{(1)}_0)^2+\\sigma_2^2\\bigr)\\right]>0.\n\\]\n\nTo state the squared-speed consequence precisely, use the \\(L^2\\)\nnorm for the vector blocks \\(Z^{(1)},W^{(4)}\\) and the\nHilbert--Schmidt norm for the two matrix velocities. Let\n\\(\\mathcal J_\\ell(T)\\) be the integral from \\(0\\) to \\(T\\) of the\nsquared velocity of block \\(\\ell\\). Equation (1) and the time change\ngive the exact identity\n\\[\n \\mathcal J_\\ell(T)\n =\\int_0^T4(1-f(s(t)))^2\\kappa_\\ell(t)\\,dt.\n\\]\nTherefore\n\\[\n \\mathcal J_\\ell(T)=\\frac{16}{3}\\gamma_\\ell T^3+o(T^3)\n       \\quad(\\ell=1,2,3),\\qquad\n \\mathcal J_4(T)=4m_3T+o(T).                            \\tag{17}\n\\]\nThe initial matrix actions need not be Hilbert--Schmidt; only their\nrank-one velocities and subsequent increments use that norm.\n\nThe hidden features themselves have positive squared-speed integrals\nas well. Equations (7) and (15) give\n\\[\n \\frac{dZ^{(\\ell)}}{dt}=4tV_\\ell+o(t),\\qquad\n \\frac{dH^{(\\ell)}}{dt}=4tD_{\\ell,0}V_\\ell+o(t),\n\\]\nand hence\n\\[\n \\int_0^T\\left\\|\\frac{dZ^{(\\ell)}}{dt}\\right\\|_\\ell^2dt\n       =\\frac{16}{3}\\|V_\\ell\\|_\\ell^2T^3+o(T^3),\n\\]\n\\[\n \\int_0^T\\left\\|\\frac{dH^{(\\ell)}}{dt}\\right\\|_\\ell^2dt\n       =\\frac{16}{3}\\|D_{\\ell,0}V_\\ell\\|_\\ell^2T^3+o(T^3).\n                                                                    \\tag{18}\n\\]\nAll six leading coefficients in (18) are strictly positive. These\nare local statements conditional on the canonical flow/action\nconstruction; they make no assertion about the extent of its horizon.\n\n## The kernel changes and the activation remains genuinely nonlinear\n\nThe expansions also prove nonconstancy of the total kernel.\nEquations (4)--(5) and adjunction give\n\\[\n \\langle\\beta_3,\\mathcal A^{(3)}_0\\beta_3\\rangle_3\n =m_2\\|\\beta_3\\|_3^2+m_1\\|B_2\\|_2^2+\\|D_{1,0}P_1\\|_1^2\n =\\gamma_1+\\gamma_2+\\gamma_3>0.\n\\]\nSince \\(H^{(3)}(s)=H^{(3)}_0+\n(s^2/2)D_{3,0}V_3+o(s^2)\\), expanding its squared norm gives\n\\[\n \\kappa_4(s)=m_3+s^2(\\gamma_1+\\gamma_2+\\gamma_3)+o(s^2).\n\\]\nIn feature time the sum of the three hidden kernel contributions\nhas the same positive \\(s^2\\) coefficient. In physical time,\n\\[\n \\kappa(t)\n =m_3+8(\\gamma_1+\\gamma_2+\\gamma_3)t^2+o(t^2).           \\tag{19}\n\\]\nHence \\(\\kappa\\) is not constant on any sufficiently small initial\ninterval. The gradient identity also gives\n\\(L(t)=1-4m_3t+o(t)\\), and \\(L(t)<1\\) for small positive \\(t\\).\n\nFor each layer the initial preactivation is a nondegenerate\nGaussian. Its variance is positive. The mean-square error of the\nbest affine approximation to the activation is\n\\[\n \\inf_{\\alpha,\\beta\\in\\mathbb R}\n E_\\ell[(\\phi(Z^{(\\ell)})-\\alpha Z^{(\\ell)}-\\beta)^2]\n =\n \\operatorname{Var}(\\phi(Z^{(\\ell)}))\n -\\frac{\\operatorname{Cov}(Z^{(\\ell)},\\phi(Z^{(\\ell)}))^2}\n        {\\operatorname{Var}(Z^{(\\ell)})}.               \\tag{20}\n\\]\nInitially (20) is strictly positive. Otherwise \\(\\arctan z\\)\nwould agree with an affine function with probability one under a\nfull-support Gaussian law; continuity would make them agree for\nevery real \\(z\\), which is false. The first and second moments\nin (20) are continuous along the constructed mean-square paths,\nbecause \\(\\phi\\) is bounded and Lipschitz. Thus the variance and\n(20) remain strictly positive on a common positive initial\ninterval for all three hidden layers.\n", "truncated": false}}

All three hidden\nlayers have width \\(n\\). The first preactivation \\(z^{(1)}\\) and the\nrescaled readout \\(W^{(4)}\\) are \\(n\\)-vectors. The two hidden matrices\n\\(W^{(2)},W^{(3)}\\) are \\(n\\) by \\(n\\). With \\(\\phi=\\arctan\\), set\n\\[\n h^{(\\ell)}=\\phi(z^{(\\ell)}),\\qquad\n z^{(2)}=W^{(2)}h^{(1)},\\qquad z^{(3)}=W^{(3)}h^{(2)},\n\\]\n\\[\n f_n=\\frac{(W^{(4)})^\\top h^{(3)}}n,\\qquad\n r_n=f_n-1,\\qquad L_n=r_n^2,\n\\]\n\\[\n \\delta^{(3)}=W^{(4)}\\odot\\phi'(z^{(3)}),\\quad\n \\delta^{(2)}=\\phi'(z^{(2)})\\odot(W^{(3)})^\\top\\delta^{(3)},\\quad\n \\delta^{(1)}=\\phi'(z^{(1)})\\odot(W^{(2)})^\\top\\delta^{(2)}.\n \\tag{1}\n\\]\nThe initialization blocks are independent, with\n\\[\n z^{(1)}_{0,i}\\sim N(0,1),\\quad\n W^{(2)}_{0,ij},W^{(3)}_{0,ij}\\sim N(0,1/n),\\quad\n W^{(4)}_{0,i}\\sim N(0,n^{-2}).\n \\tag{2}\n\\]\nUse the exact raw updates, with \\(\\eta_n=n^{-2}\\),\n\\[\n z^{(1)}_{k+1}=z^{(1)}_k-2\\eta_n r_{n,k}\\delta^{(1)}_k,\n\\]\n\\[\n W^{(\\ell)}_{k+1}\n =W^{(\\ell)}_k-\\frac{2\\eta_n r_{n,k}}n\n           \\delta^{(\\ell)}_k(h^{(\\ell-1)}_k)^\\top,\n \\qquad\\ell=2,3,\n\\]\n\\[\n W^{(4)}_{k+1}=W^{(4)}_k-2\\eta_n r_{n,k}h^{(3)}_k.\n \\tag{3}\n\\]\nPhysical time is \\(t=k\\eta_n\\). Between these times interpolate the\nraw parameters linearly and recompute all hidden preactivations and\nfeatures from the interpolated parameters. Finite gradient flow\nmeans the differential equations with the same right-hand sides\ndivided by \\(\\eta_n\\).\nAt GD mesh nodes, velocities mean right-hand derivatives; use the\nleft-hand derivative at \\(T_0\\) if it is a terminal mesh node.\n\nHere is one explicit, very conservative positive interval. Let\n\\[\n a=\\pi/2,\\quad A=a^2+e,\\quad\n M_p=2^{1/p}\\exp\\!\\big(A(2a+1)+2pA^2a^2\\big)\\quad(p=1,2),\n\\]\n\\[\n A_3=a^2+AM_1,\\quad\n C_3=(1+2a)\\exp((1+2a)A_3)+a^2,\\quad Q=a(1+C_3),\n\\]\n\\[\n C_2=(2Q+C_3)M_2+Q^2,\\qquad\n S_0=\\min\\{1,(2C_2)^{-1},(2C_3)^{-1}\\},\\qquad\n T_0=\\frac14\\min\\{S_0,(4a^2)^{-1}\\}.\n \\tag{4}\n\\]\nThe constants are deliberately not optimized. They are finite explicit\nnumbers determined by \\(\\arctan\\), not by an unproved continuation\nor moment assumption.\n\n## Conclusions on this interval\n\nThere are three fixed neuron probability spaces, with bounded initial\nmatrix actions \\(W^{(2)}_0,W^{(3)}_0\\) and their reverse actions.\nThey are constructed from the joint limits of finite Gaussian matrix\ncalculations, preserving every reused transpose. There is a unique\nlocal uncut population state\n\\[\n X^{(1)}(t),\\qquad W^{(2)}(t),\\qquad\n W^{(3)}(t),\\qquad W^{(4)}(t),\\qquad 0\\le t\\le T_0.\n \\tag{5}\n\\]\nHere \\(X^{(1)}=F(Z^{(1)})\\), \\(F(z)=z+z^3/3\\);\nthe two matrices are bounded actions between the adjacent population\nspaces; and the readout is the typical population coordinate.\nInitially \\(Z^{(1)}_0\\) is standard Gaussian and \\(W^{(4)}_0=0\\).\nThis is a finite list of evolving fields and operators, not a\nfinite-scalar description.\n\nUse (1) on these spaces, replacing finite transposes by their reverse\nactions, denoted by a star, and using ordinary pointwise products.\nThen\n\\[\n f=E_3[W^{(4)}H^{(3)}],\\quad r=f-1,\\quad L=r^2,\n\\]\n\\[\n \\frac{dX^{(1)}}{dt}=-2r\\,(W^{(2)})^*\\delta^{(2)},\\quad\n \\frac{dW^{(2)}}{dt}=-2r\\,\\delta^{(2)}\\otimes H^{(1)},\n\\]\n\\[\n \\frac{dW^{(3)}}{dt}=-2r\\,\\delta^{(3)}\\otimes H^{(2)},\\quad\n \\frac{dW^{(4)}}{dt}=-2r\\,H^{(3)}.                       \\tag{6}\n\\]\nThe rank-one action is explicitly\n\\((U\\otimes V)B=U E[VB]\\).\nUniqueness holds among continuous integral solutions on these fixed\nspaces with bounded operator and mean-square parameter norms.\nThe same uniqueness holds when restarting from a reached state on\nany remaining subinterval of the constructed interval.\n\nIn the raw coordinate \\(Z^{(1)}\\), (6) is the gradient flow of\n\\(L\\): use ordinary mean-square lengths for the vector fields and\nthe square-summed matrix length for trained matrix changes.\nThe present state alone determines its derivatives; the Gaussian\nresponse coefficients in the proof are not prescribed external\ninputs to its evolution.\n\nFor each fixed same-layer finite list of network measurements,\nthe joint empirical law of both finite GD and finite gradient flow\nconverges uniformly in \\(t\\in[0,T_0]\\), in probability, to the\ncorresponding population law. Convergence includes second moments.\nThe class includes finite compositions of the current states,\nglobally Lipschitz coordinate functions, bounded products, and\nboth orientations of both current matrices; finitely many specified\ntimes may be used jointly. It also includes the named backward\nfields in (1) and the hidden preactivation and feature velocities.\nNo coordinatewise pairing across distinct hidden layers is asserted.\n\nEquivalently, for any such finite same-layer coordinate list and any\nfixed continuous measurement \\(\\psi\\) of at most quadratic growth,\nits empirical average approaches its population expectation uniformly\nin time. Thus prediction, residual, and loss converge uniformly.\nThe four finite kernel blocks\n\\[\n \\frac{\\|\\delta^{(1)}\\|_2^2}{n},\\qquad\n \\frac{\\|\\delta^{(2)}\\|_2^2\\|h^{(1)}\\|_2^2}{n^2},\\qquad\n \\frac{\\|\\delta^{(3)}\\|_2^2\\|h^{(2)}\\|_2^2}{n^2},\\qquad\n \\frac{\\|h^{(3)}\\|_2^2}{n}\n \\tag{7}\n\\]\nconverge uniformly to the expectation formulas in\nLOCAL_GRADIENT_STRUCTURE.md.\nFor every hidden layer, the empirical law of its entire preactivation\npath converges, including second moments of the supremum norm, to\nthe law of its population path. Integrated squared velocities\nconverge to the corresponding population integrals.\n\nWith the same finite initialization, GD and finite gradient flow\nalso approach one another uniformly in the state distance consisting\nof the normalized Euclidean difference in \\(F(z^{(1)})\\), the two\nmatrix operator-norm differences, and the normalized Euclidean\nreadout difference. No operator-norm comparison across different\nwidths or between different underlying spaces is asserted.\n\nEvery hidden layer learns a nonconstant feature trajectory.\nMore precisely, there are nonzero square-integrable variables\n\\(V^{(\\ell)}\\) such that\n\\[\n Z^{(\\ell)}(t)-Z^{(\\ell)}_0=2t^2V^{(\\ell)}+o(t^2),\\qquad\n H^{(\\ell)}(t)-H^{(\\ell)}_0\n   =2t^2\\phi'(Z^{(\\ell)}_0)V^{(\\ell)}+o(t^2)\n \\tag{8}\n\\]\nin mean square, and both displayed leading variables have positive\nmean-square size. The three hidden kernel blocks are positive\nconstant multiples of \\(t^2+o(t^2)\\); hidden feature squared-speed\nintegrals have positive \\(T^3\\) leading coefficients. Explicit\ninitial Gaussian formulas are given in LOCAL_FEATURE_LEARNING.md.\nThe total kernel is nonconstant, the loss decreases, and the\nactivation's best affine-approximation error on each hidden\ndistribution remains strictly positive on a common initial interval.\n\n## How the premises are discharged\n\nThe proof is the following chain of proved lemmas, not a list of\nadditional assumptions on the original network.\n\n1. L3_FIXED_MESH_SOURCE_IDENTIFICATION.md proves the exact finite\n   Gaussian source representation, including both independent\n   matrices, both transposes, empirical training feedback, and\n   singular covariance cases.\n2. LOCAL_ACTION_SPACE_AND_FLOW.md realizes those finite calculations\n   on common population spaces and proves the fixed-clipping flow\n   and its fixed-clipping width limit.\n3. LOCAL_RESPONSE_BOOTSTRAP_AUDIT.md proves a tail bound uniform\n   in the Euler mesh and clipping level on the explicit \\(S_0\\).\n   Its displayed scalar equations are precisely the equations\n   proved in item 1 and realized by item 2.\n4. LOCAL_CUTOFF_BRIDGE.md uses this bound to remove clipping,\n   prove local uniqueness and restartability, and establish\n   convergence from the actual raw GD, not merely from a\n   transformed or population-feedback scheme. In particular its\n   stated representation premise is discharged by items 1--3.\n5. LOCAL_GRADIENT_STRUCTURE.md proves that the resulting autonomous\n   evolution is a genuine gradient flow with all four kernel\n   contributions.\n6. LOCAL_FEATURE_LEARNING.md derives the strictly nonzero initial\n   hidden movement from this flow and the initial Gaussian action\n   laws. Its local-flow premise is discharged by items 1--5.\n\nNone of these statements proves the all-finite-time continuation\nrequested in the main goal.\n\n\n---\n\n# Fixed-mesh source identification for clipped three-hidden-layer arctangent flow\n\nThis is a fixed finite-program result. Its constants may depend on the number of steps, the step size, and the clipping level. It proves neither mesh-uniform response bounds nor a continuous-time limit.\n\n## Statement and conventions\n\nFix an integer N, a feature step Delta > 0, and a smooth clipping function tau_R with bounded derivative, |tau_R(q)| <= |q|, |tau_R'(q)| <= 1, and |tau_R(q)| <= 2R. Let phi(z)=arctan(z), d=phi', F(z)=z+z^3/3. Let A_0,B_0 be independent n by n matrices with independent N(0,1/n) entries, independent of iid standard Gaussian Z^(1)_0. Initially C_0=0.\n\nConsider the exact finite-width discrete calculation\n\n\\[\nX^{(1)}_0=F(Z^{(1)}_0),\\quad\nH^{(1)}_k=\\phi(F^{-1}(X^{(1)}_k)),\\quad\nZ^{(2)}_k=A_kH^{(1)}_k,\\quad H^{(2)}_k=\\phi(Z^{(2)}_k),\n\\]\n\\[\nZ^{(3)}_k=B_kH^{(2)}_k,\\quad H^{(3)}_k=\\phi(Z^{(3)}_k),\\quad\n\\delta^{(3)}_k=C_k\\odot d(Z^{(3)}_k),\\quad\nq^{(2)}_k=B_k^\\top\\delta^{(3)}_k,\n\\]\n\\[\n\\delta^{(2)}_k=d(Z^{(2)}_k)\\odot\\tau_R(q^{(2)}_k),\\quad\nq^{(1)}_k=A_k^\\top\\delta^{(2)}_k,\n\\]\n\\[\nX^{(1)}_{k+1}=X^{(1)}_k+\\Delta q^{(1)}_k,\\quad\nA_{k+1}=A_k+\\frac\\Delta n\\delta^{(2)}_k(H^{(1)}_k)^\\top,\n\\]\n\\[\nB_{k+1}=B_k+\\frac\\Delta n\\delta^{(3)}_k(H^{(2)}_k)^\\top,\n\\qquad C_{k+1}=C_k+\\Delta H^{(3)}_k.\n\\]\n\nFor every fixed same-layer tuple of its nodes through step N, its empirical law converges in probability in W_2 to the scalar construction below. In particular, all the pairwise contractions used below converge. Covariance matrices may be singular.\n\nThere are four mutually independent centered Gaussian groups\n\n\\[\n(\\xi^{(2)}_k)_k,\\quad(\\xi^{(3)}_k)_k,\\quad\n(\\zeta^{(1)}_k)_k,\\quad(\\zeta^{(2)}_k)_k,\n\\]\n\nalso independent of Z^(1)_0, with covariances\n\n\\[\n\\mathbb E\\xi^{(\\ell)}_k\\xi^{(\\ell)}_s\n=\\mathbb E H^{(\\ell-1)}_kH^{(\\ell-1)}_s,\\qquad\n\\mathbb E\\zeta^{(\\ell-1)}_k\\zeta^{(\\ell-1)}_s\n=\\mathbb E\\delta^{(\\ell)}_k\\delta^{(\\ell)}_s,\n\\quad\\ell=2,3.\n\\]\n\nThe scalar equations are\n\n\\[\nX^{(1)}_k=F(Z^{(1)}_0)+\\Delta\\sum_{r<k}q^{(1)}_r,\n\\quad H^{(1)}_k=\\phi(F^{-1}(X^{(1)}_k)),\n\\]\n\\[\nZ^{(2)}_k=\\xi^{(2)}_k+\\sum_{s<k}a^{(2)}_{ks}\\delta^{(2)}_s,\n\\quad q^{(1)}_k=\\zeta^{(1)}_k+\\sum_{s\\le k}b^{(2)}_{ks}H^{(1)}_s,\n\\]\n\\[\nZ^{(3)}_k=\\xi^{(3)}_k+\\sum_{s<k}a^{(3)}_{ks}\\delta^{(3)}_s,\n\\quad q^{(2)}_k=\\zeta^{(2)}_k+\\sum_{s\\le k}b^{(3)}_{ks}H^{(2)}_s,\n\\]\n\nwith H^(ell)=phi(Z^(ell)), C_k=Delta sum_{r<k} H^(3)_r, delta^(3)_k=C_k d(Z^(3)_k), delta^(2)_k=d(Z^(2)_k)tau_R(q^(2)_k), and\n\n\\[\na^{(\\ell)}_{ks}\n=\\mathbb E\\frac{\\partial H^{(\\ell-1)}_k}\n                    {\\partial\\zeta^{(\\ell-1)}_s}\n +\\Delta\\mathbb E H^{(\\ell-1)}_kH^{(\\ell-1)}_s,\n\\qquad s<k,\n\\]\n\\[\nb^{(\\ell)}_{ks}\n=\\mathbb E\\frac{\\partial\\delta^{(\\ell)}_k}\n                    {\\partial\\xi^{(\\ell)}_s}\n +\\Delta\\mathbf1_{s<k}\\mathbb E\\delta^{(\\ell)}_k\\delta^{(\\ell)}_s,\n\\qquad s\\le k.\n\\]\n\nEvery derivative is a derivative of the explicit finite coordinate expression with respect to the named Gaussian source coordinate. Previously calculated deterministic coefficients and covariance parameters are held fixed. Distinct source coordinates remain distinct formal arguments even if their joint Gaussian law is singular. Coefficients themselves need not be invariant under a different off-support extension; their contracted correction is invariant.\n\n## Finite Gaussian conditioning, with two matrices\n\nWe first prove the needed source rule for a fixed finite calculation with deterministic scalar coefficients, globally Lipschitz C^1 coordinate instructions having bounded first derivatives, and finitely many independent Gaussian matrices, each reusable in both directions. The root coordinate tuples are iid with finite second moments and independent of the matrices. The initial tuple may contain both Z and F(Z); no Lipschitz assertion about F as a root-generating function is needed.\n\nCondition on the complete adaptive transcript. For one selected matrix W, write its previous observations as\n\n\\[\nWV=Y,\\qquad W^\\top U=Q.\n\\]\n\nThe other matrices cause no change to the following formula. Conditional residuals of the independent matrices remain independent: inductively, a query is measurable from the current transcript, and its newly observed answer imposes a linear constraint only on the queried matrix. Coordinate calculations reveal no further randomness.\n\nWhen the two input Gram matrices are invertible, Gaussian orthogonal projection gives\n\n\\[\nW\\mid\\mathcal H\\ \\overset d=\nY(V^\\top V)^{-1}V^\\top\n+U(U^\\top U)^{-1}Q^\\top P_{V^\\perp}\n+P_{U^\\perp}\\widetilde W P_{V^\\perp}.\n\\tag{1}\n\\]\n\nFor a new input h, put alpha_n=(V^T V)^(-1)V^T h and h_perp=h-V alpha_n. Then\n\n\\[\nWh=Y\\alpha_n+U\\beta_n+\n\\frac{\\|h_\\perp\\|_2}{\\sqrt n}P_{U^\\perp}g,\n\\quad\n\\beta_n=(U^\\top U/n)^{-1}(Q^\\top h_\\perp/n),\n\\tag{2}\n\\]\n\nin conditional law, with fresh standard Gaussian g. The transpose formula is identical with the two sides interchanged.\n\nAssume for the moment that all limiting input Gram matrices are positive definite. Induction on the finite transcript proves joint W_2 empirical convergence: all coefficients in (2) converge by the previous induction hypothesis; the removed projection has conditional mean squared normalized norm rank(U)/n; after removing it, conditional averaging of independent Gaussian coordinates gives joint weak convergence and second-moment convergence. Globally Lipschitz coordinate instructions preserve W_2 convergence. This works unchanged with two interleaved matrices.\n\n## Why the response coefficient is the source derivative\n\nHere is the identification step, rather than an invocation of a general tensor-program theorem. Use lowercase letters for the limiting scalar variables. Let the previous forward inputs be v_r, and the previous transpose inputs be u_s. Let Gamma_U=(E u_s u_t)_{st}. By induction write\n\n\\[\ny_r=\\xi_r+\\sum_s D_{rs}u_s,\n\\qquad D_{rs}=\\mathbb E\\partial_{\\zeta_s}v_r,\n\\]\n\\[\nq_s=\\zeta_s+\\text{a linear combination of previous forward inputs}.\n\\]\n\nUnavailable/future-source derivatives are zero. Let alpha be the limiting least-squares coefficients and h_perp=h-sum_r alpha_r v_r. Orthogonality gives E[v_r h_perp]=0 for every old forward input. Therefore the non-Gaussian correction in every q_s drops out of its pairing with h_perp:\n\n\\[\n\\mathbb E[q_s h_\\perp]=\\mathbb E[\\zeta_s h_\\perp].\n\\]\n\nThe Gaussian group zeta is independent of the roots and all other Gaussian groups and has covariance Gamma_U. The resulting rule is exactly\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\quad\n(Wh)_{\\mathrm{lim}}\n=\\xi_h+\\sum_s u_s\\,\\mathbb E\\partial_{\\zeta_s}h.\n\\quad}\n\\tag{3}\n\\]\n\nThe new Gaussian source is xi_h=sum_r alpha_r xi_r+sigma g_scalar, where sigma^2=E h_perp^2. Hence Cov(xi_h,xi_r)=E[h v_r] and Var(xi_h)=E h^2. The fresh scalar innovation is independent of every old source. As a result, source groups belonging to distinct oriented matrices W, W^T remain mutually independent, even though W and W^T themselves are dependent. The same argument applies separately to A_0 and B_0 at every interleaved call.\n\nThis proof uses the complete derivative of h as its finite coordinate expression. It does not discard derivative paths passing through calls to the other matrix.\n\n## Removing singular-Gram difficulties\n\nFor each matrix call, temporarily replace its input h by h+epsilon chi, where chi is a new independent standard Gaussian input vector, revealed immediately before that call. Give enough detail for the user to verify the step without reconstructing missing reasoning.\n\nIn particular:\n\n- identify the definition, identity, inequality, or prior claim being used;\n- show substitutions, rearrangements, case transitions, and changes of variables that carry real mathematical content;\n- track domains, signs, quantifiers, equality conditions, exceptional cases, and possible zero denominators;\n- justify limit exchanges, differentiation or integration under a sign, convergence claims, and optimization steps;\n- distinguish exact arguments from heuristics, approximations, and numerical evidence;\n- show that intermediate claims actually imply the requested conclusion.\n\nAvoid words such as \u201cclearly,\u201d \u201cobviously,\u201d \u201cstandard,\u201d and \u201cit follows\u201d when they replace reasoning. They are acceptable only after the supporting reason has been supplied.\n\nDo not over-explain elementary arithmetic or definitions already established. Compress routine steps while preserving the chain of verification.\n\n## Invoke external results completely\n\nWhenever the solution relies on a nontrivial theorem or external fact:\n\n1. state the exact form needed, including its assumptions and conclusion;\n2. verify each assumption in the present problem;\n3. identify the current objects substituted into the theorem;\n4. state exactly what conclusion the theorem yields here.\n\nDo not merely name a theorem or call a fact standard. Prefer the relevant specialization over an unnecessarily general statement.\n\nVerify a recent, specialized, source-specific, or uncertain result against a primary or authoritative source before relying on it. Cite the source near the claim. Paraphrase the relevant result unless its exact wording matters; quote only a short compliant excerpt when useful.\n\nIf the required theorem is unavailable, uncertain, or does not apply, expose the gap instead of proceeding as though it were valid.\n\n## Use examples and checks proportionately\n\nInclude an example, boundary case, counterexample, or remark only when it clarifies an abstraction, tests a hypothesis, explains a consequence, or exposes why an assumption is needed.\n\nUse low-cost sanity checks when they add confidence, such as:\n\n- substituting the result back into the defining relation;\n- checking dimensions, signs, or units;\n- testing a boundary or small case;\n- comparing with a known special case;\n- deriving the same conclusion by a second short route.\n\nDo not add examples mechanically or let them replace the general argument.\n\n## Keep the presentation compact\n\nUse headings only when they make a substantial solution easier to navigate. Keep notation sparse and stable. Prefer explicit expressions to disposable shorthand.\n\nUse equations to carry mathematical content, not decoration. Avoid formula dumps, decorative summaries, and boxed equations. State the conclusion plainly.\n\nLet the problem's complexity determine the answer length. Preserve every necessary assumption, theorem check, and logical transition, but remove repetition and exposition that does not improve understanding or verification.\n\n## Audit and revise silently\n\nDraft the solution, then review it before sending. Check:\n\n1. Did the solution address the strongest reasonable interpretation rather than a straw man?\n2. Were all adopted assumptions stated, and were none invented merely to force the result?\n3. Was the setup sufficient but minimal?\n4. Was every persistent symbol necessary and defined?\n5. Did a substantial proof receive a useful architecture?\n6. Can the reader verify every nontrivial transition?\n7. Was every external theorem stated in the needed form, with its hypotheses checked and its conclusion applied explicitly?\n8. Does the final conclusion answer the exact question?\n11. Do examples or remarks earn their space?\n12. Integrate theory, adversarial reasoning, and only authorized computation. Preserve uncertainty: an honest open or inconclusive result is preferable to a stronger unsupported claim.\n\nTreat the skill as the research-program controller. Use a specialized proof, teaching, paper-review, data, or coding skill for bounded subtasks when appropriate, while retaining the claim structure and evidence updates here.\n\n## Load references selectively\n\n- Read [research-contract.md](references/research-contract.md) when starting, materially reformulating, or checking the non-vacuity of a conjecture.\n- Read [evidence-ledger.md](references/evidence-ledger.md) when resuming prior work, reconciling contradictory artifacts, updating conclusions, or writing a master report.\n- Read [adversarial-audit.md](references/adversarial-audit.md) before declaring a loophole closed, a route impossible, a result decisive, or a theorem nearly established.\n- Read [decisive-experiments.md](references/decisive-experiments.md) only when computation is explicitly authorized or when the user asks for an experimental design. Use parallel agents only when the user explicitly authorizes delegation or parallel work; otherwise apply the same registry and round discipline sequentially.\n\n## Establish scope and authority\n\n1. Restate the research target in one sentence.\n2. Determine whether the user authorized:\n   - read-only synthesis or assessment;\n   - new theoretical analysis;\n   - experiment design only;\n   - implementation or computation;\n   - delegated or parallel proof search;\n   - a bounded continuation under conditional branches.\n3. Record any time, compute, token, data, model, or run budget as a hard constraint.\n4. Ask only for a missing choice that would materially change the result. Otherwise make the narrowest reasonable assumption and label it.\n5. Never expand a diagnostic or reporting request into implementation, computation, external actions, or a new research branch.\n\n## Core workflow\n\n### 1. Restore the authoritative state\n\nRead the current primary artifacts before reasoning from memory. Identify the canonical statement, latest valid methods, raw evidence, unresolved objections, and superseded conclusions. Prefer derivations and raw results over summaries; prefer audited later results only when they actually repair or invalidate earlier work.\n\nWhen resuming or synthesizing, maintain the ledger in [evidence-ledger.md](references/evidence-ledger.md).\n\n### 2. Freeze the research contract\n\nSpecify the canonical object, admissible inputs, observables, error criterion, topology or norm, horizon, limit order, approximation family, coefficient provenance, complexity dependence, and forbidden substitutions. State what information the proposed surrogate may retain and whether it must be autonomous and restartable.\n\nApply the non-vacuity checks in [research-contract.md](references/research-contract.md). Reject oracle playback, hidden encodings of the target trajectory, replacement by an easier model, or quantifiers that avoid the intended compression problem.\n\n### 3. Build the claim ladder\n\nSeparate at least:\n\n1. exact identities or finite constructions;\n2. well-posedness or internal correctness of the proposed approximation;\n3. empirical accuracy on tested instances;\n4. convergence of the approximation hierarchy;\n5. identification with the intended limit or real system;\n6. compact-horizon validity;\n7. all-time or uniform validity;\n8. existence of some admissible witness versus success of the current witness.\n\nDo not promote evidence from one rung to another without an explicit bridge.\n\n### 4. State the sharp conjecture\n\nWrite explicit quantifiers and dependencies. State:\n\n- the admissible problem class;\n- what may depend on accuracy, horizon, and regularity;\n- what must remain independent of ambient scale or inaccessible trajectory information;\n- the approximation guarantee and norm;\n- coefficient provenance and initialization;\n- autonomy, restartability, or finite-memory requirements;\n- concrete falsifiers.\n\nIf several statements are needed, identify one central conjecture and label the rest as lemmas, assumptions, or stronger extensions.\n\n### 5. Derive the exact causal skeleton\n\nDerive before truncating. Mark each step as exact, conditional on named assumptions, heuristic, empirical, or open. Track causal dependencies, information flow, history dependence, and the source of every residual.\n\nKeep distinct approximation axes distinct. Convergence in time step, basis degree, perturbation order, response depth, width, spatial resolution, or another coordinate does not imply convergence in any other axis.\n\nIn particular, separate:\n\n- correctness of every fixed-order coefficient from convergence of the full expansion;\n- production of omitted error from propagation or stability of that error;\n- observable accuracy from state-space convergence;\n- failure of a proof route from falsity of the conjecture.\n\n### 6. Build a typed evidence ledger\n\nFor each central claim, record its exact statement, claim-ladder rung, status, assumptions, supporting and contrary evidence, dependencies, cheapest resolver, falsifier, and supersession relation.\n\nUse calibrated labels. Distinguish proved, exact under assumptions, empirically supported, disfavored, falsified, open, and superseded. Never translate \u201cnot observed\u201d into \u201cruled out.\u201d\n\n### 7. Run a hostile audit\n\nAttack the strongest plausible version of each alternative, not a straw man. Check for:\n\n- hidden memory or inaccessible information;\n- tail escape and high-to-low feedback;\n- topology or observable mismatch;\n- nonnormal amplification and unstable error propagation;\n- unjustified interchange of limits;\n- easier-model substitution;\n- nuisance explanations matched only by weak controls;\n- numerical conditioning, discretization, leakage, or selection effects;\n- a result that validates one witness but not the intended existence claim.\n\nUse [adversarial-audit.md](references/adversarial-audit.md) and state what each surviving objection would change.\n\n### 8. Select one bottleneck\n\nRank candidate next steps by logical leverage, expected uncertainty reduction, mechanism relevance, and cost. Prefer the smallest step whose possible outcomes would change the research state.\n\nDo not optimize for volume of algebra, number of experiments, or apparent completeness. Avoid polishing downstream machinery while an upstream identification or compactness gap remains decisive.\n\nNormally pursue one bottleneck at a time. In an authorized multi-route proof search, retain a small structurally diverse portfolio and select one explicit bottleneck per active route using [proof-search-orchestration.md](references/proof-search-orchestration.md).\n\n### 9. Precommit any authorized experiment\n\nBefore implementation or execution, read [decisive-experiments.md](references/decisive-experiments.md) and freeze:\n\n- competing hypotheses;\n- the disputed mechanism and why the testbed preserves it;\n- primary metric and matched controls;\n- pass, fail, and inconclusive thresholds;\n- numerical validity gates;\n- replication rule and conditional branches;\n- exact budget and terminal stopping condition.\n\nUse the smallest nondegenerate testbed, not automatically the smallest instance. Do not launch exploratory grids when one theory-selected stress or ablation can discriminate the hypotheses.\n\n### 10. Update causally\n\nAfter a derivation or experiment, ask:\n\n1. What mechanism was supported, rejected, or left unresolved?\n2. Which exact ledger claims change status?\n3. Does a failure kill the broad conjecture, the current witness, one assumption, or only one proof route?\n4. Which earlier conclusion is superseded?\n5. Does the result authorize a precommitted branch? If not, stop.\n\nSalvage valid identities, tools, counterexamples, and mechanisms from failed programs. Do not preserve their invalid conclusion.\n\n### 11. Synthesize the current state\n\nLead with the strongest defensible conclusion. Report separately:\n\n- established results;\n- supported but unproved claims;\n- disfavored or falsified explanations;\n- unresolved decisive gaps;\n- superseded conclusions;\n- the single highest-leverage next action, if requested and authorized.\n\nWhen later work corrects earlier work, use the corrected result in the main narrative and record the supersession once. Do not accumulate mutually inconsistent report layers.\n\n## Decision rules\n\n- **Strong surrogate performance:** Treat it as evidence of utility, not hierarchy convergence or arbitrary-accuracy existence.\n- **A successful matched nonlinear or causal control:** Downgrade that particular mundane explanation; do not infer a theorem.\n- **A failed high-order trend:** Check parity, conditioning, common-reference comparability, and replication before inferring divergence.\n- **A correct local expansion with growing coefficients:** Preserve the local algebra while rejecting unsupported positive-horizon convergence.\n- **A stability theorem without a source estimate:** Record propagation control; leave error production open.\n- **Failure of one representation:** Distinguish failure of the explicit witness from failure of the broader admissible class.\n- **Confounded evidence:** Mark inconclusive and stop unless a resolution run was preauthorized.\n- **Budget exhausted:** Stop even when the scientific question remains open.\n\n## Output standards\n\nMatch the requested artifact. For a concise assessment, provide the current conclusion, decisive evidence, and leading gap. For a full research state, provide:\n\n1. canonical target and research contract;\n2. sharp conjecture;\n3. exact causal skeleton;\n4. claim and evidence ledger;\n5. adversarial alternatives;\n6. experimental evidence and validity limits;\n7. what is established, disfavored, falsified, open, and superseded;\n8. ranked proof obligations or next decision.\n\nKeep notation stable and minimal. Attach claims to evidence close to where they appear. State assumptions at the claim they support. Never hide a decisive gap in a generic limitations section.\n", "truncated": false}}

Exact covariance term in the scaled response energy\n\nPut\n\n    Lambda_i(s) = n E_xi ||y(s)||^2.\n\nThe Hilbert adjoint of R_s in the unweighted transformed state norm is\n\n    R_s* y = W2 x + A H1 =: gamma2,\n\nwhereas T_s y=zeta2. Define the mixed probe covariance\n\n    Gamma_(i,j)(s) = n E_xi [gamma2_j(s) zeta2_j(s)].\n\nTaking the energy of (2), using (3) and Young's inequality, gives\n\n    Lambda_i'\n      <= C_(S,M)(1+Lambda_i)\n          + 2 <phi''(z2) q, Gamma_i>.                   (4)\n\nAll inner products here are normalized middle-layer averages. Moreover\n\n    ||Gamma_i||_L1 <= C_(S,M) Lambda_i.                  (5)\n\nThe final pairing in (4) is the only coefficient not closed by the existing primal bounds in this transformed tangent calculation. It involves the covariance of a specific zero-initial-data, single-column-seeded Gaussian tangent, rather than an arbitrary variation.\n\nRank-one training removes part of it entirely. The exact history identity gives\n\n    q = W3_0* d + k,\n    ||k||infinity <= a^3 S^3/2.\n\nThe k contribution in (4) is bounded by C_(S,M)Lambda_i using (5). Thus the unresolved quantity can be narrowed to\n\n    <phi''(z2) W3_0* d, Gamma_i>.                        (6)\n\nA sufficient spatial estimate would be ||Gamma_i||2<=C Lambda_i; then the already bounded L2 norm of q closes (4). This is a delocalization statement about this particular probe covariance, and has not been proved.\n\nFor moment bounds, an even more tailored sufficient estimate is the following full-Gaussian-law inequality, for r>=1. If localization is used to obtain it, its boundary terms must be included rather than discarded:\n\n    E[Lambda_i^(r-1)\n      <phi''(z2) W3_0* d, Gamma_i>]\n      <= C E[Lambda_i^r]\n         + C r log(e+r)^2 E[Lambda_i^(r-1)].             (7)\n\nWhen the other constants are uniform, (4) and Holder imply\n\n    d/ds ||Lambda_i||_r\n       <= C ||Lambda_i||_r + C r log(e+r)^2,\n\nhence ||sqrt(Lambda_i(s))||_p<=C_S sqrt(p)log(e+p), uniformly for s<=S. Equation (7) is not established here.\n\n## 4. Why this response energy controls both deleted-query Jacobians\n\nLet bar d be the copied-top query with neuron i removed from its input, still driven by the actual bulk path. Let J_i=D_(W3_0[:,i]) bar d be its ordinary n-by-n Jacobian. Under the probe above,\n\n    dot bar d = J_i xi/sqrt(n).\n\nIts input derivative is (I-P_i)u2. The bounded copied-top variation equations give, pointwise in the actual initialization,\n\n    ||J_i(s)||HS/sqrt(n)\n      = sqrt[n E_xi ||dot bar d(s)||2^2]\n      <= C_(S,M) [sqrt(Lambda_i(s))\n                    + integral_0^s sqrt(Lambda_i(u)) du]. (8)\n\nThis follows by applying the instantaneous-plus-integrated L2 top-response estimate to (I-P_i)u2, followed by Minkowski in xi and the boundedness of T_u. In particular, it requires no exchange between a time supremum and the probe expectation.\n\nThus\n\n    |Tr J_i|/n <= ||J_i||HS/sqrt(n),\n    ||J_i^T g/n|| <= [||J_i||HS/sqrt(n)] [||g||/sqrt(n)], (9)\n\nwhere g=sqrt(n) W3_0[:,i] is the actual Gaussian column. No independence between J_i and g is used in (9). Under the full Gaussian law, |||g||/sqrt(n)||_p <=1+C sqrt(p/n). The top-response constants in (8) are polynomial in initial operator norms, whose fixed-degree moment factors are bounded when n is sufficiently large relative to p.\n\nTherefore a uniform-in-time Lp bound C sqrt(p)log(e+p) for sqrt(Lambda_i(s)), with the indicated operator-norm weights and a harmless increase of p, suffices for BOTH normalized-trace and Gaussian-direction targets in DELETED_QUERY_RESPONSE_AND_ENTROPY_AUDIT.md. Minkowski handles the time integral in (8). The reduction uses a normalized HS covariance quantity, not a full Jacobian operator-norm estimate.\n\n## 5. Gaussian integration by parts exposes a mixed second response\n\nThere is an exact reason why averaging the original Gaussian disorder does not immediately close (6). For r=1, write phi''_j=phi''(z2_j). Under justified Gaussian integration by parts,\n\n    E <phi''(z2) W3_0* d, Gamma_i>\n      = (1/n^2) sum_(a,j) E [\n          (partial_(W3_0,aj) d_a) phi''_j Gamma_(i,j)\n          + d_a phi'''(z2_j)\n              (partial_(W3_0,aj) z2_j) Gamma_(i,j)\n          + d_a phi''_j\n              partial_(W3_0,aj) Gamma_(i,j) ].          (10)\n\nThe last derivative is\n\n    partial_w Gamma_(i,j)\n      = n E_xi [\n          (partial_w gamma2_j) zeta2_j\n          + gamma2_j (partial_w zeta2_j) ].             (11)\n\nThese are mixed second derivatives of the actual causal flow: one derivative is the column probe and the other is an initial Gaussian entry. Wick averaging in xi contracts its Gaussian factors but leaves these mixed flow derivatives. For r>1, differentiating Lambda_i^(r-1) introduces further contractions with the same mixed derivatives.\n\nThe mixed second variation Z^(v,w) of a finite-dimensional flow obeys\n\n    Z' = DV Z + D^2V[U^v,U^w],       Z(0)=0.\n\nHere the second source contains, among other exact middle-gate terms,\n\n    phi'''(z2) q zeta2^v zeta2^w\n      + phi''(z2) [q_dot^v zeta2^w + q_dot^w zeta2^v].\n\nThus no closure follows merely from the Gaussianity of the probe or the rank-one form of weight training. The uncanceled term (11), with its signed contraction in (10), is a narrower next resolver than a full tangent operator bound.\n\n## 6. Relation to the new pruned-row Wishart geometry\n\nThe independent rows in a fully pruned reference can describe the scalar part of rare-layer mobility and may be useful for estimating the specific covariance Gamma_i. They cannot currently replace the actual W2, D1, gamma2, or zeta2 in (4): all of those have been propagated through the original feedback.\n\nThere is a real own-site cancellation in the scalar comparison. For z'=a(s)q(s)phi'(z), zero initial tangent, and a variation only of q, the exact derivative satisfies\n\n    zeta(s)=phi'(z(s)) integral_0^s a(u) q_dot(u) du.\n\nThe large q multiplier does not amplify this response. With an additional bulk forcing c(s), the integrating-factor equation acquires the coefficient -(phi''/phi')(z)c(s), as well as the variation of c. The rare diagonal approximation therefore isolates a useful principal cancellation, but transferring it to (4) still requires estimating the actual bulk/covariance correction. No such transfer is assumed in this note.\n\n## Conclusion\n\nA new positive fact is the exact 1/n mean-square tangent forcing and the HS bridge (8)--(9). Rank-one learned top history is also harmless in the energy. The remaining obstruction is a specified mixed covariance pairing of the actual causal tangent; original-Gaussian integration by parts converts it into mixed second-response contractions, not independent noise. Closing (7), or the stronger spatial covariance estimate following (6), would advance the global theorem. Neither is proved here.\n", "truncated": false}}

Do not exploit an omission to answer a trivial or uninteresting straw-man version.\n\nHandle ambiguity according to its effect:\n\n- If it does not change the substance, adopt the conventional interpretation and state it briefly.\n- If one reasonable assumption makes the intended problem precise, state that assumption before solving.\n- If several reasonable interpretations lead to materially different answers, ask for clarification or give a compact case split when that fully resolves the ambiguity.\n- If a missing assumption is necessary for the claimed conclusion, do not invent it silently.\n\nIf the stated claim is false, say so and give a decisive counterexample or contradiction. Present a corrected nearby statement only when it helps, and label it as a correction rather than the original result.\n\nAnswer the problem actually asked. Do not weaken a universal claim to a convenient special case, replace an exact question with a numerical approximation, or prove a converse instead of the stated direction.\n\n## Establish a minimal setup\n\nBegin with a compact setup or preliminaries passage when it reduces ambiguity or supports later reasoning. State only the necessary:\n\n- domain and assumptions;\n- definitions used in the solution;\n- boundary, regularity, integrability, independence, or nondegeneracy conditions that matter;\n- notation that must persist through the answer.\n\nReuse the problem's notation whenever possible. Introduce a new symbol only when the unabbreviated expression is genuinely cumbersome and recurs often. Define every new symbol before use and state its mathematical type when that is not immediately evident.\n\nDo not force a visible setup heading for a short elementary problem. Do not hide substantive assumptions in prose later in the solution.\n\n## Give the architecture before a substantial proof\n\nBefore a long or conceptually difficult proof, explain the plan in a short paragraph or compact list. Identify the main steps, cases, claims, or lemmas and how they combine to yield the conclusion.\n\nKeep the architecture at the level needed to orient the reader. Do not duplicate the detailed proof, and do not substitute a plan for the proof itself. For a routine calculation or one-step argument, omit the architecture.\n\n## Execute every nontrivial step\n\nDerive each nontrivial algebraic, analytic, probabilistic, geometric, combinatorial, or logical transition. Give enough detail for the user to verify the step without reconstructing missing reasoning.\n\nIn particular:\n\n- identify the definition, identity, inequality, or prior claim being used;\n- show substitutions, rearrangements, case transitions, and changes of variables that carry real mathematical content;\n- track domains, signs, quantifiers, equality conditions, exceptional cases, and possible zero denominators;\n- justify limit exchanges, differentiation or integration under a sign, convergence claims, and optimization steps;\n- distinguish exact arguments from heuristics, approximations, and numerical evidence;\n- show that intermediate claims actually imply the requested conclusion.\n\nAvoid words such as \u201cclearly,\u201d \u201cobviously,\u201d \u201cstandard,\u201d and \u201cit follows\u201d when they replace reasoning. They are acceptable only after the supporting reason has been supplied.\n\nDo not over-explain elementary arithmetic or definitions already established. Compress routine steps while preserving the chain of verification.\n\n## Invoke external results completely\n\nWhenever the solution relies on a nontrivial theorem or external fact:\n\n1. state the exact form needed, including its assumptions and conclusion;\n2. verify each assumption in the present problem;\n3. identify the current objects substituted into the theorem;\n4. state exactly what conclusion the theorem yields here.\n\nDo not merely name a theorem or call a fact standard. Prefer the relevant specialization over an unnecessarily general statement.\n\nVerify a recent, specialized, source-specific, or uncertain result against a primary or authoritative source before relying on it. Cite the source near the claim. Paraphrase the relevant result unless its exact wording matters; quote only a short compliant excerpt when useful.\n\nIf the required theorem is unavailable, uncertain, or does not apply, expose the gap instead of proceeding as though it were valid.\n\n## Use examples and checks proportionately\n\nInclude an example, boundary case, counterexample, or remark only when it clarifies an abstraction, tests a hypothesis, explains a consequence, or exposes why an assumption is needed.\n\nUse low-cost sanity checks when they add confidence, such as:\n\n- substituting the result back into the defining relation;\n- checking dimensions, signs, or units;\n- testing a boundary or small case;\n- comparing with a known special case;\n- deriving the same conclusion by a second short route.\n\nDo not add examples mechanically or let them replace the general argument.\n\n## Keep the presentation compact\n\nUse headings only when they make a substantial solution easier to navigate. Keep notation sparse and stable. Prefer explicit expressions to disposable shorthand.\n\nUse equations to carry mathematical content, not decoration. Avoid formula dumps, decorative summaries, and boxed equations. State the conclusion plainly.\n\nLet the problem's complexity determine the answer length. Preserve every necessary assumption, theorem check, and logical transition, but remove repetition and exposition that does not improve understanding or verification.\n\n## Audit and revise silently\n\nDraft the solution, then review it before sending. Check:\n\n1. Did the solution address the strongest reasonable interpretation rather than a straw man?\n2. Were all adopted assumptions stated, and were none invented merely to force the result?\n3. Was the setup sufficient but minimal?\n4. Was every persistent symbol necessary and defined?\n5. Did a substantial proof receive a useful architecture?\n6. Can the reader verify every nontrivial transition?\n7. Was every external theorem stated in the needed form, with its hypotheses checked and its conclusion applied explicitly?\n8. Were recent, specialized, or uncertain results verified from an authoritative source?\n9. Were edge cases, equality conditions, domains, and quantifiers handled?\n10. Does the final conclusion answer the exact question?\n11. Do examples or remarks earn their space?\n12. Is the answer as compact as rigor allows, with no boxed equations?\n\nRevise any failing part and repeat the audit until the answer satisfies the checklist as well as possible. Do not mention the drafting or audit process in the final answer.\n", "truncated": false}}

Valid algebra does not rescue the failed theorem.\n# Adversarial Audit\n\nUse this reference before calling a result decisive, closing a loophole, declaring a route impossible, or claiming that only technical work remains.\n\n## Audit protocol\n\nFor every central claim or proposed next step, write:\n\n| Item | Question |\n|---|---|\n| Target claim | What exact statement is under attack? |\n| Strongest alternative | What is the most plausible competing explanation or obstruction? |\n| Failure signature | What observation or derivation would distinguish it? |\n| Cheapest discriminator | What is the smallest valid theory or experiment check? |\n| Validity gates | What would make the check numerically or logically uninterpretable? |\n| Consequence | Which claim-ladder rung changes under each outcome? |\n\nAttack the strongest viable alternative. Do not use a weak baseline merely because it is easy to defeat.\n\n## Structural attacks\n\n### Hidden information and memory\n\n- Check whether coefficients, initialization, or forcing use the future target trajectory.\n- Check whether a finite coordinate hides an arbitrary function, history, matrix, dataset, or unbounded-precision code.\n- Check whether the current state determines future evolution or whether untracked response/history variables survive.\n- Test restartability from an intermediate state when autonomy is claimed.\n\n### Nonclosure and tail escape\n\n- Identify the exact residual generated by truncation.\n- Check whether bounded norm implies compactness in the required topology; Add a mechanism-specific ablation when possible.\n\nClosing a loophole requires evidence against this strongest version, not against identity dynamics or another straw man.\n\n## Numerical and rungs.\n- **Conditional:** matters only if a named assumption fails.\n- **Minor:** affects constants, presentation, or a noncentral extension.\n\nDo not call a gap \u201ctechnical\u201d unless a known theorem or fully specified argument appears to close it under already verified hypotheses.\n\n## Evidence language\n\nUse these distinctions:\n\n- **Ruled out:** logically contradicted or rejected by a valid, sufficiently powered discriminator over the stated scope.\n- **Strongly disfavored:** survives logically but conflicts with replicated evidence.\n- **Disfavored:** has contrary evidence with hostile questions\n\nBefore upgrading the research claim, answer:\n\n1. What is the strongest surviving ordinary explanation?\n2. What is the strongest structural obstruction?\n3. What numerical artifact could mimic the result?\n4. Which necessary claim-ladder bridge remains assumed?\n5. Would the opposite result have changed the conclusion?\n6. Was that decision rule fixed before observing the result?\n7. Does the evidence generalize beyond the selected instances?\n8. What would still make the central claim false?\n# Bounded Multi-Route Proof Search\n\nUse this mode to search for a complete proof of a mathematical conjecture across several genuinely different approaches. Do not treat the mode, the user's optimism, or the conjecture's fame as evidence that a proof exists.\n\n## Fix the proof contract\n\nBefore choosing approaches, record:\n\n- the exact theorem, quantifiers, hypotheses, definitions, and edge cases;\n- which classical or supplied results may be used;\n- what counts as a complete proof;\n- which special cases, reductions, computations, or conditional results do not resolve the target;\n- the time, compute, token, and concurrency budget;\n- the terminal outcomes: a proof that survives audit, or budget exhaustion with exact proved results and gaps.\n\nDo not prohibit literature search unless the user requests an independent-discovery or benchmark-integrity mode. Otherwise explore the routes sequentially with the same records and stopping rules. Never hard-code an agent count, runtime, or product-specific orchestration feature.\n\nAllocate available effort dynamically. Match the portfolio size to the budget, keep synthesis capacity in reserve, and reduce breadth when routes cannot be audited adequately.\n\n## Seed a diverse portfolio\n\nDefine approach families by mathematical mechanism, not wording. The same is true of the operator A and all its time derivatives, since A is constant.\n\n## Failure of uniform integrability\n\nFor each fixed t > 0,\n\n    integral_E |delta(t)|^2 = t^2,\n\nalthough measure(E)=epsilon tends to zero. Therefore the squared gated fields are not uniformly integrable at any positive fixed time. They are not uniformly integrable in space-time either, because\n\n    measure([0,S] x E) = S epsilon -> 0,\n    integral_0^S integral_E |delta(t)|^2 dt = S^3/3 > 0.\n\nOn E the cancellation is exact: (A delta)|_E=0, hence z|_E=0 and D(z)|_E=1. Positivity controls the total pairing <delta,A delta>, not its restriction to E. The off-diagonal contribution cancels the positive rare-coordinate contribution and transfers motion to the bulk.\n\n## Instantaneous algebraic factorization\n\nEven the algebraic form A = m_1 I + W D_1^2 W* does not by itself rule this out. On a copy of the same finite-dimensional probability space choose\n\n    z_1 = tan(1/2) pointwise,\n    h_1 = arctan(z_1) = 1/2,\n    m_1 = ||h_1||_2^2 = 1/4,\n    D_1 = cos(1/2)^2 I,\n    W = cos(1/2)^(-2) (A - I/4)^(1/2).\n\nThe positive square root exists because lambda_- > 1/4, and direct multiplication gives\n\n    W D_1^2 W* = A - I/4.\n\nMoreover ||W||_op = sqrt(lambda_+ - 1/4)/cos(1/2)^2 is width-independent. This factorization respects the arctan relation between h_1 and D_1, but it does NOT enforce z=W h_1, a Gaussian law for W, learned-weight flow equations, or the coupled evolution of z_1. It is an algebraic observation only.\n\nIf a zero initial derivative q'(0) is also desired, replace t in delta by t^2 and replace t^2/2 in z by t^3/3. The same argument and uniform bounds on every fixed interval hold, and both q(0) and q'(0) then vanish.\n\nConclusion: uniform operator positivity, bounded normalized-L2 q and q', bounded normalized-L2 z, zero initial q, and bounded total action do not imply uniform integrability of |D(z)q|^2. Additional structure from canonical Gaussian initialization and the exact coupled dynamics is essential.\n", "truncated": false}}

Select one bottleneck\n\nRank candidate next steps by logical leverage, expected uncertainty reduction, mechanism relevance, and cost. Prefer the smallest step whose possible outcomes would change the research state.\n\nDo not optimize for volume of algebra, number of experiments, or apparent completeness. Avoid polishing downstream machinery while an upstream identification or compactness gap remains decisive.\n\nNormally pursue one bottleneck at a time. In an authorized multi-route proof search, retain a small structurally diverse portfolio and select one explicit bottleneck per active route using [proof-search-orchestration.md](references/proof-search-orchestration.md).\n\n### 9. Precommit any authorized experiment\n\nBefore implementation or execution, read [decisive-experiments.md](references/decisive-experiments.md) and freeze:\n\n- competing hypotheses;\n- the disputed mechanism and why the testbed preserves it;\n- primary metric and matched controls;\n- pass, fail, and inconclusive thresholds;\n- numerical validity gates;\n- replication rule and conditional branches;\n- exact budget and terminal stopping condition.\n\nUse the smallest nondegenerate testbed, not automatically the smallest instance. Do not launch exploratory grids when one theory-selected stress or ablation can discriminate the hypotheses.\n\n### 10. Update causally\n\nAfter a derivation or experiment, ask:\n\n1. What mechanism was supported, rejected, or left unresolved?\n2. Which exact ledger claims change status?\n3. Does a failure kill the broad conjecture, the current witness, one assumption, or only one proof route?\n4. Which earlier conclusion is superseded?\n5. Does the result authorize a precommitted branch? If not, stop.\n\nSalvage valid identities, tools, counterexamples, and mechanisms from failed programs. Do not preserve their invalid conclusion.\n\n### 11. Synthesize the current state\n\nLead with the strongest defensible conclusion. Report separately:\n\n- established results;\n- supported but unproved claims;\n- disfavored or falsified explanations;\n- unresolved decisive gaps;\n- superseded conclusions;\n- the single highest-leverage next action, if requested and authorized.\n\nWhen later work corrects earlier work, use the corrected result in the main narrative and record the supersession once. Do not accumulate mutually inconsistent report layers.\n\n## Decision rules\n\n- **Strong surrogate performance:** Treat it as evidence of utility, not hierarchy convergence or arbitrary-accuracy existence.\n- **A successful matched nonlinear or causal control:** Downgrade that particular mundane explanation; do not infer a theorem.\n- **A failed high-order trend:** Check parity, conditioning, common-reference comparability, and replication before inferring divergence.\n- **A correct local expansion with growing coefficients:** Preserve the local algebra while rejecting unsupported positive-horizon convergence.\n- **A stability theorem without a source estimate:** Record propagation control; leave error production open.\n- **Failure of one representation:** Distinguish failure of the explicit witness from failure of the broader admissible class.\n- **Confounded evidence:** Mark inconclusive and stop unless a resolution run was preauthorized.\n- **Budget exhausted:** Stop even when the scientific question remains open.\n\n## Output standards\n\nMatch the requested artifact. Cluster routes that use the same mathematical idea even when their notation differs.\n\n## Enforce a concrete route contract\n\nRequire every route to return:\n\n1. a precise claim or construction;\n2. a derivation or proof of everything asserted;\n3. every external dependency and its checked hypotheses;\n4. a counterexample search or sanity check when applicable;\n5. the exact unresolved implication, if any;\n6. a registry-status recommendation and reason.\n\nReject vague progress reports, unsupported optimism, and claims that a global compatibility step is routine. A reduction is meaningful progress only when its target is already proved, strictly better understood, or accompanied by a new mechanism that attacks it.\n\n## Run adaptive rounds\n\nAfter each round:\n\n1. verify concrete outputs before treating them as progress;\n2. merge duplicate routes by mechanism;\n3. identify reductions whose missing lemma is equivalent in strength to the original theorem;\n4. redirect effort toward underexplored families or newly enabled bottlenecks;\n5. mark a route blocked when it stalls at a theorem-strength lemma;\n6. reopen a blocked route only after a materially new invariant, construction, theorem, or counterexample appears;\n7. cross-pollinate mature routes when one route supplies another's missing ingredient;\n8. preserve valid lemmas and counterexamples from failed routes.\n\nDo not let elegance, early popularity, or the amount of work already invested determine allocation.\n\n## Audit candidate proofs independently\n\nWhen a complete route appears, stop expanding it and begin reconstruction.
