The preceding bound with \\(a=1/4\\)\nand a union bound give net error at most \\(1/4\\), except on an event\nof probability at most \\(2\\exp(m\\log9-p/128)\\).\nFor any symmetric \\(A\\), approximation by this net gives\n\\(\\|A\\|_{\\rm op}\\le2\\max_v|v^\\top A v|\\). Apply this to\n\\(A=U_{[p]}U_{[p]}^\\top/p-I_m\\), proving (1).\n\nWrite \\(\\Theta_{[p]}=\\sigma U_{[p]}/\\sqrt m\\). Its effective rank is\n\\[\nr_p=\\operatorname{tr}\\!\\left[\n  \\frac{U_{[p]}U_{[p]}^\\top}{m}\n  \\left(\\frac{U_{[p]}U_{[p]}^\\top}{m}+I_m\\right)^{-1}\n\\right].\n\\]\nThe factor \\(\\sigma\\) has canceled exactly. On (1), every eigenvalue\ninside the fraction is at least \\(p/(2m)\\), whence\n\\[\n\\frac{p}{p+2m}\\le \\frac{r_p}{m}\\le1.\n\\]\nThus \\(r_p/m\\to1\\). Effective rank increases on adding columns:\nindeed \\(A\\mapsto I-(I+A)^{-1}\\) preserves the order on positive\nmatrices. Hence \\(r_p\\le r_K\\le m\\), proving \\(r_K/m\\to1\\).\n\nLet \\(A_\\theta\\) be the regularized upper Cholesky factor, and write\n\\(t_i=(\\Theta A_\\theta^{-1})_i\\). Prefix Cholesky factors agree with\nthe corresponding leading blocks, so\n\\[\n\\sum_{i\\le p}\\|t_i\\|_2^2=r_p,\\qquad\n\\sum_{i\\le K}\\|t_i\\|_2^2=r_K,\\qquad\n\\sum_{i\\le K}t_it_i^\\top\\preceq I_m.                          \\tag{2}\n\\]\nThe last identity follows from\n\\(\\Theta(\\Theta^\\top\\Theta+\\sigma^2I)^{-1}\\Theta^\\top\n\\preceq I_m\\).\n\nConditional on \\(U\\), the vector \\(g_K\\) is centered Gaussian, with\n\\[\n\\operatorname{Cov}(g_K\\mid U)\n=\\frac{B^2+\\sigma^2}{m}\\sum_{i\\le K}t_it_i^\\top.\n\\]\nIts covariance trace is \\((B^2+\\sigma^2)r_K/m\\to B^2\\) in\nprobability, and its largest eigenvalue is at most\n\\((B^2+\\sigma^2)/m\\). For a centered Gaussian vector of covariance\n\\(C\\), independence in an orthonormal eigenbasis gives\n\\(\\operatorname{Var}(\\|Z\\|_2^2)=2\\operatorname{tr}(C^2)\\).\nConsequently the conditional variance here is at most\n\\(2(B^2+\\sigma^2)^2/m\\). Conditional Chebyshev's inequality proves\n\\(\\|g_K\\|_2^2\\to B^2\\).\n\nThe exact suffix calculation also gives, for\n\\(P_K=\\eta\\sum_{l=1}^K g_l\\),\n\\[\n\\operatorname{Cov}(P_K\\mid U)\n=\\frac{\\eta^2}{m}\\sum_{i=1}^K\n \\left[B^2(K-i+1)^2+\\sigma^2(K-i+1)\\right]t_it_i^\\top.\n\\]\nIts trace lies between\n\\[\nT^2B^2\\left(1-\\frac{p-1}{K}\\right)^2\\frac{r_p}{m}\n\\quad\\hbox{and}\\quad T^2B^2+\\sigma^2T\\eta.\n\\]\nBoth bounds tend to \\(T^2B^2\\). By (2), its largest covariance\neigenvalue is at most \\((T^2B^2+\\sigma^2T\\eta)/m\\). The same\nconditional variance calculation proves the asserted convergence of\n\\(\\|P_K\\|_2^2\\).\n\n## Scope\n\nThe history is uniformly close to zero but is not uniformly\ntime-Lipschitz on this fine mesh. The smooth-history theorem therefore\nremains valid. This example rules out extending its conclusion merely\nby saying that the history has an additional \\(O(\\sigma)\\) jitter that\nvanishes uniformly. Regularized effective rank is sensitive to that\njitter when the number of queries greatly exceeds the width.\n\nThis also explains why an adaptive effective-rank bound, even if\nproved, would not automatically settle the network comparison.\nIts rank or temporal premise would have to be verified for the actual\nperturbed history, which receives fresh additive query noise.\nThe present construction is a frozen algebraic test, not a proof that\nthe canonical comparison has macroscopic perturbations, and not a\ncounterexample to the requested MF/GF limit. It does not assume the\nqueries are independent of the auxiliary Gaussian matrix. The effective\nrank premise below remains a premise for the actual perturbed dynamics.\n\n## 1. Causal setup and exact identities\n\nFix \\(n,m,K\\ge1\\) and \\(\\sigma>0\\). Let \\(\\Gamma\\in\n\\mathbb R^{K\\times K}\\) have independent standard Gaussian entries.\nLet \\(\\mathcal H\\) contain all other random arrays and seeds, jointly\nindependent of \\(\\Gamma\\). In the perturbed-original process these\ninclude \\(X,U,V\\); revealing their entire arrays initially does not\nreveal any entry of \\(\\Gamma\\).\n\nUse finite-valued measurable causal query maps with the source's order\n\\(\\theta_l\\to p_l\\to\\omega_l\\to q_l\\). The other terms are already\nmeasurable from the queries and \\(\\mathcal H\\).\n\nFor each leading history take the positive-diagonal upper Cholesky\nfactors\n\\[\nA_\\theta^TA_\\theta=\\Theta^T\\Theta+\\sigma^2I,\\qquad\nA_\\omega^TA_\\omega=\\Omega^T\\Omega/m+\\sigma^2I.\n\\]\nThe leading blocks of these factors and their inverses agree between\nprefixes. In particular \\(t_l\\) is\nknown before the fresh row and \\(s_l\\) before the fresh column.\nAn arbitrary horizon-dependent Cholesky sign convention is not allowed.\n\nPut\n\\[\n\\mathsf T_l=\\sum_{i\\le l}t_it_i^T\\preceq I_n,\\qquad\n\\mathsf S_l=\\sum_{i\\le l}s_is_i^T\\preceq I_m,\n\\quad \\rho_{\\theta,l}=\\operatorname{tr}\\mathsf T_l,\n\\quad \\rho_{\\omega,l}=\\operatorname{tr}\\mathsf S_l.              \\tag{1}\n\\]\nIndeed \\(\\mathsf T_l=\\Theta_l(\\Theta_l^T\\Theta_l+\n\\sigma^2I)^{-1}\\Theta_l^T\\), and the singular-value decomposition\ngives eigenvalues \\(d_j^2/(d_j^2+\\sigma^2)\\le1\\); the same\ncalculation applies to \\(\\Omega_l/\\sqrt m\\). These traces are the\nregularized effective ranks. They increase with the prefix, and\n\\(\\|t_i\\|,\\|s_i\\|\\le1\\).\n\nDefine the rectangular matrices\n\\[\nB_{l-1/2}=\\sum_{i\\le l,j<l}t_i\\Gamma_{ij}s_j^T,\\qquad\nB_l=\\sum_{i,j\\le l}t_i\\Gamma_{ij}s_j^T,\\qquad B_0=0.\n\\]\nTheir half-step increments are\n\\[\nB_{l-1/2}-B_{l-1}=t_l a_l^T,\n\\quad a_l=\\sum_{j<l}s_j\\Gamma_{lj},\\qquad\nB_l-B_{l-1/2}=b_l s_l^T,\n\\quad b_l=\\sum_{i\\le l}t_i\\Gamma_{il}.                        \\tag{2}\n\\]\nThe first fresh vector is conditionally \\(N(0,\\mathsf S_{l-1})\\),\nand the second is conditionally \\(N(0,\\mathsf T_l)\\), at their\nrespective preceding half-steps. Hence \\(B\\) is a rectangular matrix\nmartingale. Its increments have finite moments at every fixed finite\n\\(n,m,K\\), by (1) and the Gaussian moments. No bound on the raw\nquery norms is needed for this assertion.\n\nLet \\(g_l\\) be the forward \\(\\Gamma\\)-perturbation in (9), and\n\\(k_l\\) the reverse perturbation divided by \\(\\sqrt m\\).\nThe exact decompositions are\n\\[\ng_l=\\frac{B_l\\omega_l}{m}\n +\\frac{\\sigma^2}{\\sqrt m\\,A_{\\omega,ll}}b_l,\\qquad\nk_l=\\frac{B_{l-1/2}^T\\theta_l}{\\sqrt m}\n +\\frac{\\sigma^2}{\\sqrt m\\,A_{\\theta,ll}}a_l.                  \\tag{3}\n\\]\nFor \\(j\\le l\\), the Gram identity gives\n\\[\n\\frac{s_j^T\\omega_l}{\\sqrt m}\n=\\big[A_\\omega-\\sigma^2A_\\omega^{-T}\\big]_{jl},\n\\]\nso \\(A_{\\omega,jl}=s_j^T\\omega_l/\\sqrt m\\) for \\(j<l\\),\nand the diagonal has the additional \\(\\sigma^2/A_{\\omega,ll}\\).\nThe same identity holds for \\(A_\\theta\\). Substitution into the two\ntriangular terms of (9) proves (3), including the strict reverse sum.\nFurthermore, each diagonal obeys \\(A_{ll}\\ge\\sigma\\): its squared\nSchur complement is\n\\(\\sigma^2+x_l^T[I-X_{l-1}(X_{l-1}^TX_{l-1}+\n\\sigma^2I)^{-1}X_{l-1}^T]x_l\\ge\\sigma^2\\).\nThus both residual coefficients in (3), apart from \\(m^{-1/2}\\),\nare at most \\(\\sigma\\).\n\n## 2. Quantitative adaptive bound\n\nTake deterministic \\(R_\\theta,R_\\omega\\ge0\\),\n\\(r=\\max(R_\\theta,R_\\omega)>0\\), and \\(0<\\alpha<1\\). Set\n\\[\nE_R=\\{\\rho_{\\theta,K}\\le R_\\theta,\n       \\rho_{\\omega,K}\\le R_\\omega\\},\\quad\nu=\\log(4K/\\alpha),\\quad c=\\sqrt{2r+4u},\n\\quad v=\\log(2(n+m)/\\alpha),\n\\quad L=2\\sqrt{rv}+\\tfrac23cv.                               \\tag{4}\n\\]\nThen\n\\[\n\\mathbb P\\left(E_R\\cap\n \\left\\{\\max_h\\|B_h\\|_{\\rm op}>L\n \\ \\text{or}\\ \\max_l(\\|a_l\\|\\vee\\|b_l\\|)>c\\right\\}\\right)\n\\le\\alpha,                                                  \\tag{5}\n\\]\nwhere \\(h\\) runs over all half and full steps through \\(K\\).\nIf additionally\n\\(\\max_l\\|\\theta_l\\|\\le A\\),\n\\(\\max_l\\|\\omega_l\\|/\\sqrt m\\le C\\), then outside the same\nexceptional event, on \\(E_R\\),\n\\[\n\\max_l\\|g_l\\|\\le\\frac{CL+\\sigma c}{\\sqrt m},\\qquad\n\\max_l\\|k_l\\|\\le\\frac{AL+\\sigma c}{\\sqrt m}.                 \\tag{6}\n\\]\nThese norm bounds may instead be imposed on an event and intersected\nwith \\(E_R\\). If \\(r=0\\), both Gram contractions are zero on\n\\(E_R\\), and the claimed perturbations are zero there.\n\n### Proof, including localization and truncation\n\nFirst stop accepting increments permanently before a rank threshold\nwould be exceeded. Before row \\(l\\), both \\(\\rho_{\\theta,l}\\)\nand \\(\\rho_{\\omega,l-1}\\) are known; accept the row only while they\nare within their thresholds. Before column \\(l\\),\n\\(\\rho_{\\omega,l}\\) is also known; accept the column only if its\nthreshold has not been exceeded. These acceptance indicators are\npredictable at their respective half-steps. The accepted process agrees\nwith \\(B\\) on \\(E_R\\). Its coefficients still refer to the original\nadaptive histories; this construction does not alter the query dynamics.\n\nFor an accepted untruncated row increment \\(X=t_la_l^T\\), its two\nconditional second-moment matrices are\n\\[\n\\mathbb E[XX^T\\mid\\mathcal F_{l-1}]\n =\\rho_{\\omega,l-1}t_lt_l^T,\\qquad\n\\mathbb E[X^TX\\mid\\mathcal F_{l-1}]\n =\\|t_l\\|^2\\mathsf S_{l-1}.\n\\]\nFor an accepted column increment \\(Y=b_ls_l^T\\), they are\n\\[\n\\mathbb E[YY^T\\mid\\mathcal F_{l-1/2}]\n =\\|s_l\\|^2\\mathsf T_l,\\qquad\n\\mathbb E[Y^TY\\mid\\mathcal F_{l-1/2}]\n =\\rho_{\\theta,l}s_ls_l^T.\n\\]\nSumming along each realized path, (1) and the threshold rule imply\n\\[\nW_{\\rm left}\\preceq\n R_\\omega\\sum_{\\rm accepted\\ rows}t_lt_l^T\n +\\sum_{\\rm accepted\\ columns}\\|s_l\\|^2I_n\n \\preceq2R_\\omega I_n,\n\\]\n\\[\nW_{\\rm right}\\preceq\n \\sum_{\\rm accepted\\ rows}\\|t_l\\|^2I_m\n +R_\\theta\\sum_{\\rm accepted\\ columns}s_ls_l^T\n \\preceq2R_\\theta I_m.                                      \\tag{7}\n\\]\nIn particular both predictable quadratic variations have norm at most\n\\(2r\\). The unequal left/right constants matter: no factor \\(K\\)\nhas been introduced.\n\nTo bound increments without an unjustified Gaussian boundedness\nassumption, multiply each accepted row increment by\n\\(\\mathbf1_{\\{\\|a_l\\|\\le c\\}}\\), and each accepted column\nincrement by \\(\\mathbf1_{\\{\\|b_l\\|\\le c\\}}\\). Conditional\nGaussian symmetry makes the truncated increments centered. Their\nconditional second moments are bounded in positive-semidefinite order\nby the untruncated ones, so (7) remains valid. The contract prevents a formally true statement from evading the scientific question.\n\n## 1. Canonical target\n\nRecord the following before choosing a proof strategy or surrogate:\n\n| Field | Required specification |\n|---|---|\n| Object | Exact system, process, operator, distribution, or model |\n| Admissible class | Inputs, parameters, regularity, data, and initial conditions |\n| Dynamics or relation | Update rule, flow, equilibrium condition, or map |\n| Observables | State components or derived quantities to approximate |\n| Error | Norm, metric, probability mode, and reference object |\n| Horizon | Fixed time, compact interval, asymptotic regime, or all time |\n| Limits | Exact order of size, depth, step, sample, or continuum limits |\n| Approximation family | Permitted state, equations, basis, memory, and operations |\n| Provenance | Information from which coefficients and initial data may be computed |\n| Complexity | What may scale with accuracy, horizon, or regularity |\n| Invariance | What must not scale with ambient system size or a hidden oracle |\n| Restartability | Whether the approximation must continue from its current state |\n| Forbidden substitutions | Easier architectures, norms, limits, observables, or optimizers |\n| Authorization | Read-only, theory, design, compute, and budget constraints |\n\nIf a field is immaterial, say why rather than silently omitting it.\n\n## 2. Non-vacuity filters\n\nReject or explicitly exclude a candidate statement if it permits any of the following:\n\n1. **Trajectory playback:** Encode the answer as a time-indexed forcing, interpolation table, or oracle coefficient.\n2. **Hidden full state:** Call a representation \u201cfinite\u201d while one coordinate contains an unbounded function, history, matrix, dataset, or arbitrary-precision code for the original system.\n3. **Instance memorization:** Choose coefficients after observing the target trajectory unless system identification is explicitly the scientific problem.\n4. **Quantifier inversion:** Prove existence separately for each realized trajectory when a uniform construction over a problem class is required.\n5. **Ambient scaling:** Let state dimension or coefficient complexity grow with the system size that the approximation is meant to compress.\n6. **Blind metric:** Measure an error that can be small while the named observables or mechanism are wrong.\n7. **Easier-model substitution:** Change the architecture, dynamics, data geometry, optimizer, scaling, or limit order that defines the question.\n8. **Noncausal initialization:** Initialize from future observations or unavailable latent variables.\n9. **Nonrestartable closure:** Match a curve from time zero but fail to evolve from an intermediate state when autonomy is part of the claim.\n10. **Unbounded precision loophole:** Store arbitrary information in finitely many real numbers without a regularity, computability, or provenance restriction.\n\n## 3. Claim ladder\n\nWrite separate propositions when the following are logically different:\n\n| Rung | Claim |\n|---|---|\n| A | An exact identity or finite truncation is well defined |\n| B | The truncated or surrogate dynamics are internally well posed |\n| C | The surrogate matches tested instances |\n| D | Successive approximations converge in the stated topology |\n| E | The hierarchy limit equals the intended mathematical limit |\n| F | The approximation is valid on every compact horizon |\n| G | The approximation is uniform or stable for all time |\n| H | Some admissible finite witness exists |\n| W | The particular proposed witness succeeds |\n\nDo not use evidence for C to assert D, or failure of W to reject H.\n\n## 4. Sharp-conjecture template\n\nAdapt this template rather than copying it mechanically:\n\n> Let \\(\\mathcal C\\) be the stated admissible class and let \\(O[S](t)\\) be the named observable of the canonical system \\(S\\). For every accuracy \\(\\varepsilon>0\\), horizon \\(T<\\infty\\), and required regularity bound \\(R\\), there exists an admissible autonomous approximation \\(A_{\\varepsilon,T,R}\\) of complexity \\(N(\\varepsilon,T,R)\\), independent of the ambient scale and of the realized future trajectory, whose coefficients and initial state are computable from the permitted source data, such that\n> \\[\n> \\sup_{S\\in\\mathcal C_R} d_T\\!\\left(O[S],O[A_{\\varepsilon,T,R}[S]]\\right)\\le \\varepsilon.\n> \\]\n> The approximation remains restartable from its finite state and obeys the stated limit order and provenance restrictions.\n\nThen specify:\n\n- whether the bound is deterministic, in probability, almost sure, or in expectation;\n- whether \\(N\\) may depend on the data dimension, sample count, or other fixed structural quantities;\n- whether one construction works uniformly over \\(\\mathcal C_R\\);\n- what computable or regular coefficient class excludes real-number oracle encodings;\n- what observation map compares the approximation to the target.\n\n## 5. Falsifiers and witnesses\n\nName concrete outcomes with distinct logical force:\n\n- **Witness falsifier:** disproves the current representation or closure.\n- **Mechanism falsifier:** rejects a proposed reason for convergence or success.\n- **Uniformity falsifier:** exhibits a family on which required complexity or error escapes.\n- **Existence falsifier:** proves no admissible approximation in the full stated class can work.\n- **Proof-route falsifier:** invalidates one argument while leaving the conjecture intact.\n\nFor each, state the exact assumption or rung it affects.\n\n## 6. Contract-change rule\n\nWhen evidence suggests changing the problem:\n\n1. Preserve the original contract.\n2. State the proposed change and scientific reason.\n3. Explain whether it weakens, strengthens, or replaces the conjecture.\n4. Obtain user direction when the change is material.\n5. Never present results for the revised contract as answers to the original one.\n", "truncated": false}}

## Conjecture: autonomous three-hidden-layer mean-field gradient flow

Let \(\phi(z)=\arctan z\). Consider a network with one input and target, both equal to \(1\), and three hidden layers of width \(n\). Its parameters are
\[
z^{(1)}\in\mathbb R^n,\qquad
W^{(2)},W^{(3)}\in\mathbb R^{n\times n},
\qquad W^{(4)}\in\mathbb R^n.
\]
Here \(z^{(1)}\) is the first-layer weight vector evaluated at the input, and \(W^{(4)}\) is the rescaled output weight.

At step \(k\), define
\[
h_k^{(\ell)}=\phi(z_k^{(\ell)}),\qquad
z_k^{(2)}=W_k^{(2)}h_k^{(1)},\qquad
z_k^{(3)}=W_k^{(3)}h_k^{(2)},
\]
\[
f_{n,k}=\frac{(W_k^{(4)})^\top h_k^{(3)}}n,\qquad
r_{n,k}=f_{n,k}-1,\qquad L_{n,k}=r_{n,k}^2,
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\delta_k^{(3)}
&=W_k^{(4)}\odot\phi'(z_k^{(3)}),\\
\delta_k^{(2)}
&=\phi'(z_k^{(2)})\odot
       (W_k^{(3)})^\top\delta_k^{(3)},\\
\delta_k^{(1)}
&=\phi'(z_k^{(1)})\odot
       (W_k^{(2)})^\top\delta_k^{(2)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The activation and its derivative act coordinatewise; \(\odot\) denotes coordinatewise multiplication.

Initialize all entries independently, across and within parameter blocks:
\[
z_{0,i}^{(1)}\sim N(0,1),\qquad
W_{0,ij}^{(2)},W_{0,ij}^{(3)}\sim N(0,n^{-1}),\qquad
W_{0,i}^{(4)}\sim N(0,n^{-2}).
\]
With \(\eta_n=n^{-2}\), train every block by the exact updates
\[
\begin{aligned}
z_{k+1}^{(1)}
&=z_k^{(1)}-2\eta_n r_{n,k}\delta_k^{(1)},\\
W_{k+1}^{(\ell)}
&=W_k^{(\ell)}
-\frac{2\eta_n r_{n,k}}n
 \delta_k^{(\ell)}(h_k^{(\ell-1)})^\top,
&&\ell=2,3,\\
W_{k+1}^{(4)}
&=W_k^{(4)}-2\eta_n r_{n,k}h_k^{(3)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Use physical time \(t=k\eta_n\), interpolate the raw parameters linearly, and recompute the hidden quantities from them. The corresponding finite-width gradient flow replaces these updates by their differential equations. These dynamics use normalized Euclidean squared lengths for the vector blocks and ordinary Frobenius squared lengths for the matrix blocks.

**Conjecture.** The following unconditional statement holds.

There exist three fixed probability spaces \((\Omega_\ell,\mu_\ell)\), independent of width and time horizon, supporting a population state consisting of exactly
\[
Z^{(1)}(t),\qquad W^{(2)}(t),\qquad
W^{(3)}(t),\qquad W^{(4)}(t).
\]
Here \(Z^{(1)}\) and \(W^{(4)}\) are square-integrable scalar fields on \(\Omega_1\) and \(\Omega_3\), respectively, and
\[
W^{(\ell)}(t):L^2(\Omega_{\ell-1})\longrightarrow L^2(\Omega_\ell),
\qquad \ell=2,3,
\]
are bounded linear operators. Write \(\mathbb E_\ell\) for integration over \(\Omega_\ell\), and \((W^{(\ell)})^*\) for the adjoint, characterized by
\[
\mathbb E_\ell[U\,W^{(\ell)}V]
=
\mathbb E_{\ell-1}[V\,(W^{(\ell)})^*U].
\]

Define the population forward and backward quantities by the finite-network formulas above, replacing \(z,h\) by \(Z,H\), transposes by adjoints, and
\[
f(t)=\mathbb E_3[W^{(4)}(t)H^{(3)}(t)],
\qquad r(t)=f(t)-1,\qquad L(t)=r(t)^2.
\]
The evolution is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\dot Z^{(1)}&=-2r\,\delta^{(1)},\\
\dot W^{(\ell)}U
&=-2r\,\delta^{(\ell)}
       \mathbb E_{\ell-1}[H^{(\ell-1)}U],
&&\ell=2,3,\quad U\in L^2(\Omega_{\ell-1}),\\
\dot W^{(4)}&=-2r\,H^{(3)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Initially \(Z_0^{(1)}\sim N(0,1)\) and \(W_0^{(4)}=0\). The joint initial operator actions must reproduce the Gaussian initialization through the empirical-convergence requirement below at \(t=0\), including arbitrary finite reuse of both matrices and their transposes. Each probability space is generated by these initial measurement fields; it may not contain additional information encoding the future training trajectory.

On these fixed spaces, the equations have a unique global continuous integral solution, with locally bounded field second moments and operator norms. The solution is uniquely restartable from every reached state. The four displayed objects constitute the entire evolving state: no external time-dependent coefficients or additional history are supplied.

Moreover, this is the gradient flow of \(L\), with squared length of a parameter variation given by
\[
\mathbb E_1[(dZ^{(1)})^2]
+\|dW^{(2)}\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2
+\|dW^{(3)}\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2
+\mathbb E_3[(dW^{(4)})^2].
\]
Here \(\|A\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2=\sum_j\mathbb E_\ell[(Ae_j)^2]\) for an orthonormal basis of the input space—the operator counterpart of squared Frobenius norm. The trained matrix increments, not necessarily the initial operators themselves, have finite such norm on every compact time interval.

The finite GD and finite gradient-flow systems converge jointly to this same population evolution as \(n\to\infty\), along the full sequence, in the following sense.

Take any fixed finite collection of same-layer vector measurements formed from the parameter fields and constants using:

- fixed globally Lipschitz coordinate functions and multiplication by bounded globally Lipschitz coordinate functions;
- normalized inner products;
- any finite, layer-compatible composition of the current matrices and their transposes.

The instructions are independent of \(n\). The collection may also include the named backward fields, hidden preactivation and activation velocities, and measurements at finitely many other fixed times. Population measurements use the same instructions, with expectations and adjoints replacing normalized inner products and transposes.

For every such collection \(v_n^1(t),\ldots,v_n^m(t)\), every continuous \(\psi:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) satisfying
\[
|\psi(a)|\le C\left(1+\sum_{j=1}^m a_j^2\right),
\]
and every fixed \(T<\infty\),
\[
\sup_{0\le t\le T}
\left|
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\psi\!\left(v_{n,i}^1(t),\ldots,v_{n,i}^m(t)\right)
-
\mathbb E_\ell
\psi\!\left(V^1(t),\ldots,V^m(t)\right)
\right|
\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}0.
\]
This applies jointly to GD and finite gradient flow started from the same initialization, with corresponding limiting fields identified. GD velocities use right derivatives at mesh points and the left derivative at a terminal mesh point. No coordinatewise pairing between different neuron layers is asserted.

The empirical laws of entire hidden preactivation paths also converge: for every continuous function \(\Psi\) on \(C([0,T])\) of at most quadratic growth in the supremum norm,
\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\Psi(z_{n,i}^{(\ell)}(\cdot))
\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}
\mathbb E_\ell[\Psi(Z^{(\ell)}(\cdot))].
\]
In particular, predictions, losses, integrated squared hidden velocities, and all four kernel contributions
\[
\left(
\frac{\|\delta^{(1)}\|_2^2}{n},\
\frac{\|\delta^{(2)}\|_2^2\|h^{(1)}\|_2^2}{n^2},\
\frac{\|\delta^{(3)}\|_2^2\|h^{(2)}\|_2^2}{n^2},\
\frac{\|h^{(3)}\|_2^2}{n}
\right)
\]
converge to their corresponding population expressions; the time-dependent quantities converge uniformly on \([0,T]\).

Finally, every hidden layer undergoes nontrivial feature learning:
\[
0<
\lim_{t\downarrow0}
\frac{\mathbb E_\ell[
|H^{(\ell)}(t)-H^{(\ell)}(0)|^2]}{t^4}
<\infty,
\qquad \ell=1,2,3.
\]

Prove or refute this conjecture as stated. A refutation must contradict a specified conclusion for the prescribed Gaussian-initialized system; failure of a particular proof strategy or a counterexample with different initialization does not suffice.
